description: Two actors begin an improvised scene. At any point another player calls 'Freeze', tags out one of the two actors, takes their exact physical position, and starts a brand-new scene justifying that pose. Can be played fast (quick-wit warm-up) or with scenes allowed to develop for minutes before tagging.

A long-form improv format by Del Close: opening (audience suggestion + group association/game), then three rounds of three thematically-linked scenes, with improv games interspersed between rounds. Scenes increasingly connect and may merge by the final round. For up to ~12 players; actors play multiple roles.

One player is a party host; the other players are guests assigned secret characters or quirks by the audience. Guests arrive giving subtle behavioral clues; the host must guess each guest's identity/quirk. Game ends when the host has guessed all guests. Minimum 3 players.

Extended Freeze Tag for 4 players. Player 1 mimes an activity; 'Freeze' is called and player 2 builds a new scene from the frozen pose. Players 3 and 4 enter the same way, each new scene springing from the prior frozen position. Once all four are in, the game reverses: each 'Freeze' returns players to their earlier frozen poses until player 1 completes the original activity.

A two-or-more player scene of 26 lines of dialogue where each successive line must begin with the next letter of the alphabet (start anywhere, e.g. R, then S, then T...; after Z comes A). Players who hesitate or use the wrong letter 'die' and are replaced, the replacement taking over the same character. Story quality is prized over slavish letter-adherence.

A group sits in a circle and collaboratively tells a story by contributing exactly one word each in turn; players may say 'period' to end a sentence. Harder than it looks with beginners, so practice first with a known fairy tale. Variation: split into two circles and race to finish a story.

A narrative scaffolding exercise (Kenn Adams) for building a complete story arc using set prompts: 'Once upon a time... Every day...' (routine), 'But one day...' (disruption), 'Because of that...' (repeated consequences), 'Until finally...' (climax), 'And ever since then...' (new normal). Teaches improvisers to advance stories through change.

Players stand in a circle; one is 'Big Booty', the rest are numbered. Big Booty sets a 4-beat rhythm chanting 'Big Booty', then passes in 2 beats ('Big Booty to 7'); that number passes on within 2 beats. On any error the group says 'Oh Shit', re-chants, the erring player becomes Big Booty, numbers are reassigned, and play restarts. Concentration/warm-up for 4+.

Circle warm-up for 3+. One player makes the bunny 'body' (arms in front, hands hanging) while the two neighbors wave hands as 'ears'; all three chant 'bunny bunny bunny'. The body throws the bunny to another player who becomes the new body, with new neighbors as ears. Played fast for energy; variations swap in a car, cow, or washing machine with their own sounds.

Acceptance warm-up for 3+. The group picks a shared activity (e.g. throwing a party). A player says 'Let's...' and mimes a suggestion; everyone replies 'Yes, let's!' and performs it together. Players take turns adding 'Let's...' ideas, all of which are accepted and acted out. Teaches building on offers rather than blocking. With an imaginary product it becomes 'The Ad Game'.

Two players: one is an 'expert' on an audience-chosen subject from a foreign country who lectures entirely in gibberish; the second translates the nonsense into real language in real time. Variation: the expert tells a story instead of lecturing while the translator renders it as coherent narrative.

Players line up and the audience supplies verbs, hobbies, and occupations. Each performer steps forward to demonstrate the worst conceivable way of doing or being that thing, then steps back. A fast, short-form gag game prizing comedic execution over story.

Four chairs form a car. A driver picks up a hitchhiker who plays a strong character tic or emotion; the driver and any passengers adopt that trait. New hitchhikers board one at a time, each bringing a new trait the whole car takes on; when full, someone must leave (and must justify their exit). A character-endowment game for 4+.

One player narrates a slide show of a big activity or journey (e.g. a jungle trek, building a house) while the other players freeze into living images for each 'slide'. The slide-makers don't just illustrate the narration but extend it, showing the next step, so the story is co-built by narrator and images. 3+ players.

An audience volunteer stands on stage as 'the pillar'. Players perform a scene but can stop mid-sentence at any point and ask the pillar to supply the next word, which they must incorporate and continue. Requires 2-3 scene players plus the volunteer.

A scene is played by on-stage actors who may speak but make no other sounds; one or more off-stage players supply all sound effects. The sound team should drive and enhance the scene creatively rather than just back it. Performance game.

One player leaves the room while the audience picks a famous/historical person; the player returns and gives a press conference not knowing who they are. The other players are journalists whose questions feed clues until the player guesses their identity. Variation: use an expert/subject instead of a person. 3-8 players.

One player is the Narrator who mimes a typewriter and starts the scene by reading aloud what they 'type'; other performers act it out. The Narrator can retake control, change locations, add characters, insert flashbacks or tilts, and can mime ripping out pages to restart a scene that goes bad. 2+ players.

Players perform a scene and may hesitate mid-line at any time to ask the audience for a word, which they must accept and justify into the scene (e.g. 'hand me that...' then use whatever is shouted). Builds adaptability and acceptance of outside offers.

Four players: two perform an improvised story entirely in gibberish while two others act as translators who speak the 'subtitles' in real time. The actors feed elements to the translators and the translators steer the action back, co-building the story. Also known as Subtitles.

One group of actors plays a scene silently, mouthing words but making no sound, while another group of 2+ players sitting in front provides all the spoken dialogue. The deliberate desync of mouth and voice mimics a badly dubbed foreign film for comic effect. 2+ actors.

Two or three players perform a one-minute scene in which one player must die. Players are encouraged to take bold risks (e.g. drop dead after five seconds) and let partners improvise a justification for the death. A timed/limitations performance game.

Players line up; the audience gives a title and genre. The MC points to one player who starts narrating and switches to another player at any moment - even mid-word - who must continue flawlessly. Hesitation, bad grammar, or nonsense gets the audience yelling 'Die' and eliminates the player; the last player ends the story. Also called Conducted Story.

The stage is divided into four zones, each assigned an emotion. Performers improvise a scene and must adopt the emotion of whichever quadrant they currently stand in, moving deliberately to force emotion changes and justifying each shift. A limitations/performance game.

A line-up verbal-wit game. The audience gives a noun (e.g. 'chocolate milk') and each performer steps forward to complete 'Sex with me is like [noun]: ...' with a punchline (e.g. 'hot and sweet'). Rapid-fire one-liners under pressure; related to World's Worst and One Eighty Five.

6-15 players. Two players start a scene from an audience suggestion; any other player can call 'Cut' to interrupt and start a fresh scene, bringing one or more players along. This repeats until all scenes have been cut; interrupted scenes resume later and all eventually weave into one story. Most players keep one character. Usually set in a soap/drama genre; also called Soap.

A scene is started and a director interrupts at any point to fast-forward or rewind to another point in time; the performers then continue from that new moment using flash-forwards and flashbacks. Also called Rewind; related to Director's Cut.

Two-player exercise. One player makes any sounds with voice and body; the partner moves in synchronization with that 'soundtrack'. After a while they swap. Variations: the mover controls the sound-maker, or players freely trade lead without a fixed order. Association/concentration warm-up.

Four players sing an improvised song about an audience-given subject to the tune of 'Da Doo Ron Ron', making up both lyrics and fitting the recognizable structure. Variation: add invented choreography and dance while singing. A musical performance game.

Like Simple Continuation but the MC interrupts the scene several times, and at each interruption all actors in the scene swap roles/positions with each other; no actors join or leave. A continuation/performance game. Also called Actor Switch.

Two players perform a short scene (~8 lines each), then replay it under new constraints from the audience: a new emotion (Emotion Replay), a different era (Through the Ages), a new location, a film/TV/literary style (Style Replay), gibberish, or reversed order (Backwards Scene). A time-compression variant (Countdown/Half Life) shrinks the scene to 1 min, then 30s, 15s, 7s, 3s. Often the dialogue must stay exactly the same.

Circle warm-up; one player in the middle closes eyes, points at someone and says 'Bippety Bippety Bop' fast. The pointed player and their two neighbors must build an elephant (pointed player makes the trunk by holding nose and threading the other arm through; neighbors make big ears) before the middle player finishes the phrase. Anyone too slow becomes 'it'. Variants use cars, cows, washing machines, bunnies.

Players say the first thing they think of in response to whatever the previous player offers (heard, seen, felt, smelled, tasted). Any association is valid as long as it is not preconceived and genuinely springs from the prior offer. Core exercise underlying variants like Free Association Circle/Lines, Walk-over Association, Word Ball, and Firing Squad.

Circle association warm-up for 3+. One player tosses a word to another; the receiver says an association and throws it to someone else, and so on. Variations: combine with Last Letter or Free Association Lines, toss an actual soft object, or run multiple words at once.

A 'victim' faces a line of players. Each player in turn shouts a word and the victim must instantly reply with the first word that comes to mind, until everyone has fired one. Variation: rotate the victim to the back of the line and promote the next player; or run several victims at once. A fast association/warm-up. 2+ players.

Circle concentration/energy warm-up. A clap is passed around the circle to the right; once smooth, players may reverse direction by clapping back to whoever sent it. Variations: clap at different heights, multiple claps with movements, or simultaneous claps among pairs/trios/quads.

Two players face each other and take turns initiating slow movements (arms, legs, eyebrows) that the other mirrors exactly. It's a game of give-and-take with no continuous leader; movements stay slow. Group Mirror expands it to a whole circle mirroring one another. Concentration warm-up.

Pairs exercise from Augusto Boal. One player holds an open hand 2-3 inches from the partner's face and moves it slowly around the space; the partner keeps a constant distance, face 'magnetized' to the hand. Swap roles after a few minutes. Variation: use both hands. Builds trust, focus and leading/following.

Group icebreaker. Players stand in a tight circle, put their hands into the center, and grab two random hands. Without letting go, the group works together to untangle itself back into a circle (sometimes resolving into several smaller circles). Builds teamwork and communication.

Players line up. Player 1 mimes an activity; Player 2 asks 'What are you doing?' and Player 1 names a different, unrelated activity (e.g. while miming a haircut, says 'reading the newspaper'). Player 1 leaves, Player 2 mimes that named activity, and the cycle continues. Fast 2-player variant eliminates anyone who hesitates, says 'um', or repeats. Association warm-up.

Group exercise. The MC names a real or imaginary machine and each player becomes one moving, sounding part of it; together they coordinate to show how the device works. Variations: overdrive (machine speeds up until it explodes) or power loss (it slows to a stop). 3-4+ players.

Two teams mime a tug-of-war. Two rules: the mimed rope must not stretch or shrink, and one side must gladly lose so somebody wins (an exercise in accepting and supporting others' choices). Variations: pairs, or men vs women.

A limitations exercise (1-2 min): performers play a complete scene using only a single line of dialogue total, conveying everything else (gratitude, affection, apology) through body language, expression and action. Facilitator warns when ~20 seconds remain. Builds nonverbal communication.

Endowment game. Two performers narrate each other in the third person and assign each other do-able actions. E.g. Player 1: 'I want a divorce.' Player 2: 'she said, grabbing a knife' (Player 1 must grab a knife), then Player 2 speaks and Player 1 endows the next action, etc. With 4 players two narrate while two perform; with 3, one director and two performers.

A scene in which every line spoken must be a question; questions should still give information and advance the story, building on prior facts. Anyone who uses a statement is booed/'Die'd and replaced, the replacement taking over the same character. Limitations/performance game.

Energy circle game. A 'Whoosh' is passed around with both hands; 'Wow' (arms down) reverses direction; 'Zap' (pointing) sends it across to anyone; 'Groovelicious' makes the whole group bend down and up grooving before restarting; 'Freakout' sends everyone screaming to the center to reform the circle. Invent your own sounds/gestures. Also called Zip Zap Zoop.

One performer leaves; the host gets an everyday activity from the audience and the group changes five things about it (object, action, location, character, plus a famous-person element). The performer returns and the group plays the scene in gibberish, helping the guesser identify all five changes within five minutes through wordless acting. Gibberish/guessing game, 3+ players.

Group singing warm-up. Players form a circle; one steps to the center and sings a recognizable song. As soon as they falter, forget lyrics, or tire, another player jumps in with a different song. Not about improvising songs but about ensemble support and trusting that someone will relieve you. 3+ players.

Association warm-up: instead of naming the first word you associate, you name the first word starting with the last letter of the word you just heard. Pairs well with Walk-over Association or Word Ball.

A scene in which each new line must start with the last letter of the previous line. Performers balance meaningful dialogue with the constraint, often producing creative or comic word choices. Limitations/performance game, ~2-4 players.

Two players exchange lines that must rhyme: one delivers a line, the partner answers with a rhyming line, then offers a new line to rhyme, and so on. Players who hesitate or fail to rhyme 'die' and are replaced; story quality trumps forcing a bad rhyme. Related to Verses.

During a scene the MC rings a bell or says 'Ding' whenever a player says or does something, and that player must immediately replace it with a different line or action. Can be the opposite, or e.g. the same line in a new emotion. A spontaneity drill; use sparingly in shows. Also called New Choice / Other Choice.

A scene played in verse: every player must make their own lines rhyme with themselves (internal rhyming couplets). Pairs well with a Shakespearean style. Limitations/performance game; related to Rhymes.

Four players sing about an audience topic to an Irish-sounding tune, one line each, four lines per verse. Verse two is started by player 2, and so on, until everyone has both started and ended a verse. Optional choreography. Popularized by Whose Line Is It Anyway?

Group circle game over a beat (beatbox or track). The first player raps a line in rhythm; each next player adds a rhyming line. When someone fails to rhyme, misses the beat, or stalls, everyone yells 'Dang' and a new round starts. Non-rappers join in to shout the anticipated rhyme word at the end of each line. Sing-song warm-up, 3+ players.
A long-form sung format: a Straight Story performed as a full musical, opening with a big number and ending with a big finale, with sung songs woven through the narrative. Singing-based long form.

Four players each wear a playing card on their forehead (visible to others, not themselves). They improvise a scene where the characters' status order is set by the cards; through endowment, each player learns their own status from how others treat them. Best in a hierarchy-rich setting like a royal court. Status game.

Each performer secretly picks a status number from 1 (highest) to the number of players; duplicates allowed. They play a scene trying to embody their chosen status without knowing others' picks, producing funny clashes - especially when several pick highest or lowest. Status/performance game, best with 3+.

Pairs exercise. Players take turns giving each other commands entirely in gibberish; the receiver may not act until they understand and execute the command. Meaning must come from vocal tone, delivery, and the imagined environment - not mime. Use simple requests (e.g. 'pass the salt').

Improvise a whole scene in gibberish with no translation; the audience should still follow it and mentally translate. Keep the story extremely simple, establish the scenario fast, use real gibberish (not silent mime), and convey meaning through tone, physicality, and context. Cures over-explaining.
Two players: a foreign poet recites a poem in gibberish and a translator renders it, ideally preserving the number of lines, meter, and rhymes. Gibberish/performance translation game.

One performer leaves while the audience picks an occupation. On returning, the player is endowed by the others' behavior and dialogue with that job's traits until they guess the profession. Endowment/guessing game.

The audience supplies a location, a murder weapon, and a victim's occupation. The absent player returns and must deduce all three from the other players' physical and verbal endowment cues. Endowment/guessing game.
The audience names 3-5 objects. Through environmental suggestion and endowment, the players subtly steer another performer into using those specific objects during the scene. Endowment game.
Two players each receive a secret about themselves that the other knows but they don't. Through actions and dialogue, each tries to make the other discover their own secret. Endowment/guessing game.

The audience invents a superhero (e.g. 'Toothbrush Woman') with two strengths and one weakness. Through endowment the players guide another performer to discover the hero's identity and powers. Endowment/guessing game.

Four players. One gets a silly problem (e.g. 'my shoelaces are untied') and a simple object (e.g. a kitchen cabinet) from the audience. They play the problem unsolved and summon a hero named after the object ('Kitchen Cabinet Woman'), who enters with high status, makes it worse, drops in status, and calls the next hero. The last hero finally solves it. A 'pimping' game like Mr. So and So.

One player covers their ears while each other player collects one prediction from the audience. The player becomes a fortune teller and, characterized through the others' endowment, delivers the collected predictions. Variation: off-stage players 'possess' the fortune teller like ghosts to feed tips. 3+ players.

Short-form musical game for 2+. The audience gives a silly problem; player 1 enters as a patron and explains their woes to the bartender in an improvised song, and player 2 (the bartender) responds in another improvised song working toward a comic resolution.

Four players. One leaves while the audience endows the other three with character traits (e.g. stupid, dangerous, egomaniac). The returning player asks each of the three contestants three questions and, from the answers, tries to guess each one's assigned trait. Endowment/guessing game modeled on a TV dating show.

Two groups. The first group plays a scene from a well-known story, fairy tale, or historical fact; the second group replays the same scene in a different emotion, age, or style; then group one replays it in yet another way, alternating multiple times. Replay/performance game; related to Scene Replay and Replay Gibberish.

exercise_name: Last Line / First Line Last Line
description: The audience supplies a line (any line); players perform a scene that must end exactly on that line. The fuller version, First Line Last Line, takes both an opening and a closing line and the scene must begin and end on them. Limitations/performance game.

Everyone mills about the room; any player may stop walking at any time, and the instant one stops everyone must freeze. Once all are still, the group resumes walking - aim for the fastest synchronized freeze. Harder variation: make sounds (hum, whistle) while moving. Also called Statues; related to Walking by Numbers.

Long form for 4-12. The audience gives five themes/objects/emotions/locations/situations. Round 1: five unrelated scenes. After each round the audience eliminates one, the survivors continuing and linking, until two remain and merge into one final scene in round 5. Played with or without props/director. The no-elimination three-scene version is Triptych / Tapestry.

Icebreaker. Players walk around; the facilitator calls out a configuration like '3 noses' and players rush to form groups touching that body part together. Calls escalate ('7 left big toes', '2 earlobes', '9 fingers') until everyone is giggling. Builds comfort in a new ensemble.

Two improvisers each wear similarly sized hats and play a realistic scene; the scene ends when one player grabs (or tries and misses) the other's hat. Every grab, feint, or defensive move must be justified within the scene. Variation: ban grabbing for the first 20 seconds so the scene can establish. A very silly performance game.
Two players. One gives three unconnected sentences; the other tells the shortest possible story that incorporates all three, weaving them together with minimal extra narration. Narration exercise.

exercise_name: String of Pearls (Story String / Beads on a String)
description: Best with 7-8 players. One player gives an opening line and stands far left; another gives an (ideally unrelated) closing line and stands far right; the rest fill in middle sentences at random positions, not left-to-right. After each addition everyone recites the whole story start to finish. Optional title/genre/lines prompt. Also called Story String or Beads on a String.

Long-form/object-work format. Actors lie down and 'pop up' from the page as a narrator tells the story or introduces the next scene; the narrator can 'pull the tab' or 'turn the wheel' to trigger action, and page turns serve as edits. Narrator and actors share responsibility for justifying the story; players can even pop up as props for object work.

Players improvise a scene that a narrator describes and comments upon (like Typewriter without the typewriter). Also called Attenborough after nature-documentary narration. Narration/performance game.

Circle game. On a signal everyone picks one of three poses+sounds - Alien (antenna fingers, 'bleeb bleeb', leaning in), Cow (bend forward, hand on belly, 'moo'), or Tiger (claw hand forward, roar) - trying to all match the same one. Repeat until everyone synchronizes. Teaches cooperative 'chivalry'. Variations: invent custom animals, or play majority-wins elimination.

Circle physical warm-up for 3+. The Samurai raises a katana with a Japanese-sounding grunt; the two neighbors swing their swords at the Samurai's sides grunting in pseudo-Japanese; when they retract, the Samurai lowers the sword and makes eye contact with another player who becomes the new Samurai. Start slow, speed up.

Circle concentration warm-up. Count to 7 waving the right arm in rhythm, then 7 with the left arm, the right leg, and the left leg. Repeat the whole cycle counting down to 6, then 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 for each limb. Builds coordination and focus.

Group warm-up. Everyone starts squatting in a circle and counts 1 to 10, raising volume and intensity gradually - barely audible at 1, shouting at full volume standing with arms up at 10. Watch each other to stay synchronized; keep the build smooth.

Physical warm-up. Players stand relaxed and make figure-eight movements with progressively larger body parts: left toe, foot, leg; right side; left finger, hand, forearm, arm; right side; both arms in opposite directions; pelvis, shoulders, head; finishing with as many body parts moving in eights at once. Loosens the body.

Circle warm-up for 4-5+. One player makes a gesture+sound to their right neighbor, who copies it exactly, then turns right and creates a totally new gesture+sound to pass on. Don't preplan - commit fully. Variations: pass to anyone, or skip the imitation and just create-and-pass fast. Also called Pass Catch.

A long-form opening. Take an audience suggestion; each player in turn praises it; then praise again while endowing it with human attributes; then expand the language (poetic, gibberish-french, etc.). Players then adopt the characters that emerged and play the long form using them.

A long-form format (Armando Diaz). It opens with a storytelling monologue based on an audience suggestion; players then perform improvised scenes inspired by the monologue, and the monologue may resume later to spark more scenes.
A long-form format: a single continuous story that takes place in one location for the whole performance. Can be combined with Harold or Straight Story structures.

A long-form format (after Schnitzler): a chain of two-person scenes where at each switch the older character leaves and a new one enters with the remaining character, rotating until the last and first characters finally meet. Uses Freeze-Tag-style transitions to reveal a character across different relationships. 3+ players.

A long-form format (iO Chicago). Start with one long, well-developed scene; follow it with shorter scenes that connect to the first via returning characters, people/situations merely mentioned, or the same location - reusing and re-exploring the opening's elements. The first scene must be rich enough to build on.
The most basic long-form structure: a series of scenes, connected or not. A flexible framework for stringing improvised scenes into a show.

exercise_name: Goon River (Spoon River / Moon River / Spork River)
description: Long-form monologue format for 3-4. Players line up, take one suggestion, and tell a shared story through first-person monologues - each introduces their character, then as 'things start to happen' each reflects on events from their own perspective and adds to the story, weaving in earlier details until it winds down. Great monologue practice; often ends Spoon-River-style with a death. Short-form cousin: Voices From Heaven.

Two players (Keith Johnstone). An interrogator throws random unconnected elements at a suspect who must incorporate them and get into ever more trouble; the crime is never established. The interrogator can summon Boris, a huge invisible thug, to 'torture' the suspect (mimed), or his evil twin Igor. For laughs the suspect can even incriminate Boris. Spontaneity/justification exercise.

Name-learning circle warm-up. Each player says their name with a distinct gesture per syllable (e.g. 'Ma-' / '-ry'); the group repeats it, then recites all previous names and gestures, the chain growing with each new person. Verbal+physical+memory icebreaker.

In a scene, any player can call freeze, step out, and reveal their character's private inner thoughts to the audience before the scene resumes (other characters unaware). Reveals the gap between behavior and inner life. Variation: off-stage players speak the inner monologues, also called Alter Ego or Consciences.

Pairs gibberish warm-up. Two players face each other; one speaks gibberish with a specific emotion (angry, happy, in love) and the partner instantly copies that emotion in their own gibberish. Don't copy the actual sounds and never pause - both keep talking. After ~10 seconds the responder switches emotion and the partner mirrors it. Builds emotional responsiveness.
A neutral scene is played and frozen repeatedly by the MC; each time it resumes, all players take on a new audience-suggested emotion. Continuation/performance game building emotional range.

About 4 players. Take a family-activity suggestion and play a normal scene until characters and relationships are clear; then freeze, pick a player, and get an audience emotion for them; resume with that player embodying it, justifying why. Repeat until everyone has an emotion. Limitations/performance game.

Long form for large groups. A gathering of many characters (occasion and characters from the audience); one is the detective (optional sidekick), one the victim. Lights dim and the victim is found dead; the detective interviews each suspect (who make themselves look guilty while denying it, implicating others or playing flashbacks); finally the detective names the killer, and the murder replays in slow motion. Min roles: detective, victim, 3-4 suspects.

Inverted Q&A wit game. Players cover their ears while the audience gives questions and answers, but only the answers are kept. Players get one answer at a time and must invent the worst/silliest/funniest question that could lead to it (e.g. answer 'Yellow' -> 'What color is a school bus?'). Like World's Worst.
Ask an audience member their birthday and read their horoscope from a magazine; players then improvise a scene inspired by that horoscope. Can be combined with Day in the Life. Performance game.

Three players pick a mundane activity (brushing teeth, washing a car) and stage it as an Olympic/world-championship event: one is the athlete, the other two run a TV studio interviewing the trainer and commentating. Usually the athlete fails miserably. Optional post-event interview, dramatic replays, and multiple camera angles. Also called SloMo World Champion.

Slow-motion combat warm-up. Each player's right forearm is a poisoned sword; players fight in slow motion, blocking only with the right arm. If any other body part is touched by an opponent's sword, you must die a gruesome slow-motion death without speeding up - teaching restraint and 'chivalry'. Also called Poison Arms.

Circle association game (best with an odd number). One player makes up a gibberish word and passes it to the right; the neighbor instantly translates it into a real word; then makes a new gibberish word for the next player, and so on. Translate from the word's overall sound, parts of it, the giver's intonation, or body language. Variations: translator both translates and creates the next word; add origin languages/accents.

A scene-building technique: any player calls freeze, steps out, and describes some detail of the scene/environment to the audience without disrupting the action, then unfreezes and resumes. Use sparingly to add narrative or comic subtext. Related to Asides.

A scene played in the dark, relying entirely on sound. Because movement is noisy, it's often done as a radio play with all players seated, providing the dialogue and background noises. Limitations/look-and-listen game; related to The Bat.
Players are blindfolded and play a scene, relying on hearing and other senses; builds trust and listening. Intense variation: play barefoot with mousetraps set on the stage (called Mousetraps).

Object-work exercise for 2+. One player starts an activity that establishes a location (e.g. typing = office); the others become objects in that space (plant, door, table). The first player uses any props they recognize; afterward they identify the objects created. Performance variant: players become needed objects on demand (e.g. a chair to sit on).

Four players in two pairs. Two players are 'puppets' who speak the dialogue but cannot move themselves; the other two are puppet masters who control all of their puppet's physical movement. Requires tight coordination per pair. Variation: use audience members as puppets or masters.

Four players make two characters: each character is one player who does the voice with hands behind their back, plus a player standing behind them who provides the 'hands'. The story should be a give-and-take between voices and hands. Variant: two players supply the arms, one each. Limitations/performance game.

All players in a circle, one in the middle improvising a monologue. Any player may smoothly step into the middle and take over the monologue, continuing the thread without breaking character. Builds character, listening, and seamless continuation. Best with a larger group.

The audience gives three rules - physical (e.g. one arm), linguistic (e.g. avoid a letter), or behavioral (e.g. yell a phrase after every question) - and players run a scene obeying all three at once. Limitations game; also called Ahab and the Whale.

Concentration exercise (a Walking by Numbers variant). Players spread around the room; at any moment exactly one person must be walking and one making sound (can be the same or different people). Focus is 'given' when a walker stops or 'taken' when someone else starts walking, forcing the first to stop. Add multiple walkers for difficulty.

Concentration warm-up. Players spread out where they can all see each other; exactly one person starts walking, and whenever that person stops, exactly one (and only one) other person starts walking. Increase difficulty by allowing several walkers at once. Builds group awareness; related to Group Freeze.

Two-player limitations exercise: a player may only speak when they create a brand-new object together with a movement; established objects stay put, and merely moving an existing object doesn't grant speech. Forces strong object work and physicality. Related to Touch to Talk.

Even number of players. Each gets an animal, with two players secretly sharing the same animal. Players act out activities as their animal (eating when hungry, drinking when thirsty, grooming, fighting, sleeping, mating) and try to find their matching partner; then the group checks the pairings. Variation: assign human character types instead. Character exercise.

Players walk as themselves, then pick an inspiration - an emotion, occupation, stereotype, animal, or object - and change their walk accordingly, then develop it into a full character (personality, background, mannerisms) by associating off the walk. Related to Fast Food Laban.

Two-player exercise. Each performer is secretly given a subtext/hidden motivation (e.g. 'you want to seduce the other', 'you are a nerd', 'you want to impress people', 'you are a pessimist') that drives their behavior in a scene. Discuss realistic behavior first; aim for truthfulness, not exaggeration. Can be done solo. Character work.

One player is a seated monarch; the others enter one at a time to present offerings. The monarch responds 'Continue' (interested, come closer), 'Die' (bored, dismissed), or 'Freeze' (maybe - hold until unfrozen), rejecting for any reason. The game ends when a player gets close enough to touch the monarch. Best when the monarch is deliberately demanding. Status game, 3+ players.

Character-from-movement exercise (Keith Johnstone, after Laban). Players move combining three axes - timing (sudden/sustained), weight (heavy/light), space (direct/indirect) - producing the eight Laban efforts (punch, slash, wring, press/push, dab, flick, glide, float). They explore a quality, then ask 'who would this person be?' (e.g. a vertical mover = a general). Attributes attach to the character, not the actor's body type.

Character exercise. Players walk in silence while the facilitator names trait dimensions (high/low status, loud/silent, caring/careless, strong/weak, confident/insecure, etc.); each player notes their own natural setting, then moves as the complete opposite across all dimensions and plays scenes staying true to that inverted character.

Counterpart to Imitate. A shopkeeper builds a character that is the total opposite of the customer's - contrasting voice (loud/soft, harsh/gentle), status, age, occupation, and movement (see Fast Food Laban). A looking/listening exercise for the shopkeeper. 2 players.

Beginner environment exercise for 4+ in two rows. Player 1 mimes a door (or gate, curtain, etc.); Player 2 watches until they understand the location, enters, and delivers one line establishing where they are; Player 1 answers with one line accepting it; the scene ends. After two lines the audience should know the location, who the characters are, and their relationship. Add sound effects (a submarine door vs an elevator). Related to Three Line Environment.

Long-form format (after the film Slacker, a variation on Follow the Leaver): the scene's location may only change when a character leaves the current scene and enters a different one, so the 'camera' follows characters from encounter to encounter.

Four players play two characters. The stage is split down the middle by an impassable wall; when an actor exits one side, the other actor playing that same character enters from the other side, keeping the character consistent across performers. Develops character consistency and spatial awareness. Limitations/performance game.

Two players establish a full scene in exactly three lines (A-B-A): the first player speaks twice, the second once. In those three lines they must set the Platform - who they are, where, when, and why. Builds efficient scene setup and strong physicality. Related to Doors.

Endowment/guessing game (2+). One player leaves while the others and audience set four things: location and time, the character's identity/occupation, a physical handicap, and a personal problem. The player returns and, through the others' acting, must deduce all four without explicit clues (e.g. a limping vacuum salesman in 2050 Red Square who quotes prices in rubles). Related to Hijacker.

Character/object-work exercise. Each player thinks of someone they know and mimes how that person comes home from work - showing the home space (tidy or messy), their actions (changing, showering, eating - and what food), their mood, and how their day went. Variation: enter other locations/scenarios. Builds specific behavioral character work.

Imagination/physical warm-up. Give players an oxygen mask, then guide them to move through ever-denser substances: thin air, mist, warm water, oil, honey, Jell-O, wet cement, hard cement - feeling the mist between their fingers, honey in their hair. End frozen in cement, then break out with a big bang. Builds commitment to imaginary environments.

Spontaneity exercise. Players perform a short scene, then replay the identical scene while silently repeating a mantra (e.g. 'I'm so happy, I'm so happy') and notice how the emotional tone shifts. Try other mantras ('I hate you') or let performers choose their own. Related to Mantra Introduction; from Impro for Storytellers.

Icebreaker. Players mill about greeting each other, starting with handshakes, then in ever more specific ways set by the facilitator - as a long-lost friend, an ex-lover, someone you hate, or as characters (cowboy, soldier, nanny, Russian farmer). Also called Hello or Lost Friend.

Circle concentration warm-up. A Mexican wave of raised-and-lowered arms travels one direction around the circle while, simultaneously, names are passed the opposite direction (point at your left neighbor and say your own name). Coordinating two opposite circular patterns at once is deliberately confusing. 4-5+ players.

Two groups of up to 6 mime a volleyball game. Each player, as they pass the mimed ball, shouts the name of another player who must catch and pass it on. The mimed ball must stay visible at all times. Name-learning/mime icebreaker.

Name-learning icebreaker. One player is a zombie who moves slowly, arms outstretched, toward a target. Before the zombie reaches them, that player must shout someone else's name to redirect the zombie. Anyone tagged before naming someone becomes the new zombie. Builds spontaneity.

Energy game for 6+. Players form linked pairs (arms hooked); one is the cat, one the mouse. The cat chases the mouse; if caught, roles reverse. The mouse can hook onto either end of a pair to be safe, and the player at the far end of that pair becomes the new cat (the old cat becomes the mouse).

Energy game. Everyone starts as an egg (hands joined above head) and pairs off to play Rock Paper Scissors. Winners evolve up the chain - egg -> chicken (wings, clucking) -> dinosaur (roaring) -> Ultimate Person (arms up like Superman); losers devolve one step. Players seek same-level opponents and keep playing to rise. Uses Rock Paper Scissors as its engine.

Circle object-work warm-up. Players pass an imaginary ball one at a time while the facilitator side-coaches changes - heavier (a ton), lighter, huge, tiny, in any combination - and the players must show each property in how they handle and pass it. Builds object work and physical commitment.

Acceptance/association warm-up for 3+. A player points at another and says 'Did you hear about...'; the pointed player says yes and heightens the claim; the group gasps or giggles, then someone else restarts. Rumors escalate from mundane ('soup') to absurd. Builds agreement and listening.

Audience-participation game. The MC interviews a volunteer about their job, home, hobbies, commute, and relationships, then the cast improvises a scene of a typical day in that person's life using the details. Variation 'Nightmare' asks about fears and dislikes and stages a worst-case version of their day.

Line-up verbal-wit game. The MC collects confessions from the audience (from 'I vote democratic' to 'I sold a kidney'). A player steps forward, delivers a confession in character, and another player jumps in with a witty response; the exchange continues until it dries up, then a new player and confession rotate in. Quick-wit and comic timing.

Two players (interviewer and guest) perform a TV interview on an audience topic entirely in reverse: the first line spoken is actually the interview's closing line ('Thanks for that enlightening explanation') and they work backward to the opening. Extends to a general Backwards Scene with physical comedy. Limitations/performance game.

Long form for 4+ (2 cops, a suspect who is the victim's best friend, a victim). The audience names the victim and friend and how long they've been friends. Cops interrogate the suspect, and each question triggers a flashback scene from the answer; the show alternates interrogation and (non-chronological) flashbacks, ending when the cops ask 'Did you do it?' and the lights cut before the answer. About the relationship, not the murder.

Solo musical game. The audience names an unlikely place to find a lounge singer (e.g. 'a pediatrician's office') and one performer improvises a complete Sinatra-style lounge song about it. A great opener.

Two singers plus an audience member. Briefly interview the volunteer (name, family, job, interests), then improvise a song about them with one rule: only the singer the audience member is looking at may sing, and the moment they look at the other singer, that one takes over. Look-and-listen musical game.
Ask the audience for something that annoys them, then improvise a 70s-style anti-establishment protest song about it, in verse-chorus form. Musical performance game.

About 4 players. Two host a TV commercial for a compilation CD on an audience-given theme (e.g. accountants); they hype it and announce 3-4 track titles each implying a musical style (e.g. 'The IRS Blues'); the other players then improvise each song in that style. Popularized by Whose Line Is It Anyway?; related to CD Shop.

Pretentious-coffee-house poetry game. The audience gives two unrelated objects/concepts; each performer improvises a rhyming poem incorporating both. Miss a suggestion or fail to rhyme and the audience yells 'Die!', sending you off in a dramatic comic on-stage death. Limitations/performance game.

Two or more players build a poem one line at a time: player 1 gives the first line, player 2 the second, and so on. Experiment with forms - limerick, sonnet, haiku - to vary difficulty. Verbal-wit performance game.

Open a fortune cookie, read the fortune aloud, and improvise a scene inspired by it. Variation: give every player a fortune that they must embody through their character in the scene. Limitations/performance game.

Line-up verbal-wit game. The MC gathers famous people (living or dead) or fictional characters from the audience, and each player invents and delivers witty 'famous last words' for the given subject. Builds comic timing and wit.

4-10 players. Get a movie title from the audience; two players run an interview in which one reviews the film while the other players act out scenes and characters from it as the discussion continues. Narration/performance game.

4-6 players perform a scene; the audience votes one out, and the remaining cast replays the whole scene covering everything that happened, picking up the eliminated player's parts. This repeats until one player remains and delivers the scene solo (as a monologue or playing all characters). A strong listening/attention exercise.

Four players spoof the talent show: a host, a harsh judge, and two contestants. Contestants are introduced and each performs an improvised musical number on an audience suggestion; the judge mocks each performance. Musical performance game.

Long-form format (National Theatre of the World, Toronto): a known local writer supplies the first two pages of a non-existent novel, read aloud (ideally by the author), and the improvisers create the rest of the story on the spot. Note: the format is copyrighted - permission required to perform.

Up to 15 players line up, each with an audience-given topic. The leftmost starts a monologue; at any point any other player can 'steal' the last 3-4 words to start or continue their own monologue. Speak fast to keep your words. Performance/warm-up game.

Each character in a scene is identified by a specific hat. The MC periodically pauses and redistributes the hats; whoever now wears a hat takes on that character, and the story must continue coherently through the swaps. Optional: characters acknowledge the strange spatial jumps (sparingly). Also called Bermuda Triangle.

Two-player (or circle) object-work exercise. One player creates a precise imaginary object and passes it; the partner first stays truthful to what was built, then physically transforms it (bend, break, twist, stretch, shrink) into something new through believable transitions and passes it back. Circle variant passes morphing objects around the group.

A neutral scene is interrupted repeatedly by the MC; after each interruption the scene continues in a new audience-suggested style (film, literary, drama, TV genre), while the platform and story carry on flawlessly. Continuation/performance game.

Musical long form needing a skilled musician. The audience gives ~10 song styles and a story premise; the performers play the story straight while the musician weaves in every requested musical genre across the scene. Format/limitations sing-song game.

Icebreaker circle game. Each player holds up ten fingers; players take turns making 'I have never...' or 'I have...' style personal statements (e.g. 'I have a cat', 'I have never stolen anything'), and anyone for whom the statement is true (or who can't answer affirmatively) lowers a finger. Last player with fingers still up wins. Helps a new group learn about each other.

Scene-initiation drill. Two players start a scene that is cut after exactly three lines of dialogue; the goal is to establish as much as possible as fast as possible - platform, characters, environment and each player's motivation - then drop it and start a totally new scene, repeating. Builds efficient scene openings.

Acceptance/concentration warm-up. One player starts a small gesture with a little sound; each player around the circle tries to copy exactly what they saw, and as the gesture inevitably mutates (an arm becomes a leg, a new sound creeps in) players accept the changes rather than correcting them. Teaches acceptance and observation.

Limitations/performance game. The audience gives an adjective (e.g. 'sad') and all players perform a scene expressing that quality as fully as possible. Variation: give each performer a different adjective so contrasting qualities collide within one scene.

Physicality drill. A player performs a scene; on the trainer's clap they must make whatever they are doing more interesting without advancing the action (e.g. opening a briefcase becomes an elaborate piece of business). Variation 'Advancing and Expanding' lets a second clap permit advancing. Builds Chaplin/Mr-Bean-style physical comedy.

Trust exercise. One player is blindfolded and the room is filled with obstacles; the rest of the group verbally guides them through the course. The blindfolded player may only move forward (but can turn) and is allowed two brushing contacts with obstacles - a third collision fails the run. Also called Airplane, Obstacle Course, or Mine Field.

Concentration warm-up. Players stand in a circle and throw letters of the alphabet to one another in order, starting at A and racing through Z as fast as possible. Any group size; large groups can split into timed teams. Variation: any player can switch the sequence between the alphabet and the numbers 1-10.

Word-fluency warm-up. Players sit in a circle; one holds a ball or knotted towel and must name as many words as possible starting with a chosen letter (e.g. P) while the ball is passed around - doubles don't count. Variation: pair up with a stopwatch and run 15-20 second rounds, one partner generating words while the other counts.

Concentration circle warm-up. The group chants 'Ali Baba and the 40 Thieves' to set a rhythm; one player makes a gesture on the beat then passes it on while inventing a new one, and each player in turn takes over the previous player's gesture while the originator creates fresh. The chain of handed-down gestures grows, demanding sustained focus.

Circle movement warm-up. One player starts a dance; the others copy it, and once the initiator feels the group has it down, they stop and pass the lead to their right-hand neighbor, who invents a new dance. The lead travels around the circle, building energy through imitation and fresh invention.

Four-player status/ensemble exercise in which the group naturally forms alliances that leave one player excluded - the exclusion should emerge organically, not be forced. The excluded player accepts it and may make funny comebacks that get ignored. Variation 'Alliances' lets the excluded player recruit others to shift who is left out.

Group narrative game. One player stands in the middle; the seated players take turns assigning actions for them to perform, and after each the middle player asks 'What happens next?' to prompt the next instruction, building a coherent story. The middle player only executes; the seated players drive the tale. Also called And Then.

Character game. The audience gives animals which performers use as inspiration for characters in a scene - not literally becoming the animal but borrowing its movement, voice, or behavior (a chicken might inspire a jittery, cowardly character). Variation 'Totems' hands out animal names on slips before the scene.

Concentration warm-up. All players but one sit in a circle of chairs; the middle player calls out a description (e.g. 'all women', 'all blondes') and everyone it applies to must jump up and find a new chair, the one left standing becoming the next caller. Calling 'Fruit Basket' makes everyone swap at once. Also called Anyone Who or Train Wreck.

Three-player exercise: one is clay, one a model, one the artist. The model strikes a pose the clay can't see; the artist must sculpt the clay into that pose without touching the clay, speaking, or demonstrating. The model then checks the match. Variation: time-limit the artist. Builds nonverbal communication.

Warm-up for 7+. Each player secretly picks one other person as their 'bodyguard' and another as their 'assassin', then moves to keep the bodyguard between themselves and the assassin at all times, producing chaotic milling. After a few minutes players reveal their secret choices.

Physical association exercise. Players move freely around the room; the trainer calls a player's name and they jump into a frozen pose (the trainer may add a quality like horizontal, up, down, big, small, light, heavy). The other players then build a still scene around that frozen player. Best preceded by the simpler Jump exercise.

Long-form performance format: a collection of improvised scenes built around the making of a movie. A key role is the Director, who can stop weak scenes, redirect players, and inject plot or comedy. Optional behind-the-scenes subplots and a Typewriter-style scriptwriter. Variations 'At the Movies' and 'At the Oscars' launch the show from an Oscar nomination or win.

Trick story game. Half the group leaves while the rest learn hidden rules (e.g. answer 'no' to any question beginning with a vowel or a form of 'to be', and switch to 'yes' after two consecutive 'no' answers). The guessers ask only yes/no questions believing a story exists; their own questions unwittingly generate one until they 'solve' it. From Keith Johnstone.

Paired trust/movement exercise. Two performers stand back-to-back, backs touching, and dance together through various musical styles; the one rule is that their backs must stay in contact throughout no matter how the music changes. Builds coordination and nonverbal communication.

Two-player listening exercise. Partners do a slow dance together, each with their head on the other's shoulder, while playing a 2-3 minute scene; because they can't see each other it forces deep listening and breaks physical awkwardness. Variation 'Back to Back' plays the scene seated back-to-back with characters free to move.

Musical storytelling game. One player is the balladeer who sings an improvised ballad on an audience suggestion while the other performers act out what is sung in slow motion; the actions inspire the lyrics and the song guides the action, co-building the story. Scales into longer-form structures.

Energy warm-up tag. One player is 'it'; each tagged player must hold a 'bandaid' (their hand) on the exact spot they were tagged. After three tags a player freezes until two others simultaneously tag them and count to five to free them. Any group size.

Quick-wit warm-up circle. A caller in the middle shouts a letter and the targeted player must instantly name three things starting with it: a person's name, a sellable object/service, and a place (e.g. for B: 'Barney sells Bread in Bulgaria'). Hesitate or fail and you become the new caller.

Listening/vocal warm-up. Players are secretly assigned animals in groups of three to five sharing the same animal, then spread out and make only their animal's sound (no words) to find their group; the first group to gather all its members and sit down wins.

Physicality/imagination exercise. Players physically embody an inanimate object or abstract concept ('a jar of mayonnaise', 'water'), expressing its qualities through movement. The facilitator first prompts with questions (open or closed? full or empty?) then players develop their own analytical prompts. Any number, simultaneously or in turn.

Performance game and Fast Forward variant. Performers play a short scene; the host then asks the audience whether they want to see what happened before or what happens after that scene, and the players improvise the chosen segment, exploring the story's timeline.

Long form for 4-6. An evil character lures 3-5 guests to an abandoned place at a set time. Part one: individual scenes introduce each guest and why they accept the mysterious invitation. Part two: all arrive together and learn that by night's end all but one will die; they try to escape, survive, or overthrow the captor. Ends when one guest is freed, the guests are forgiven after learning the truth, or the captor is captured/killed.

Advanced pairs warm-up combining mirroring and storytelling. Partners set a beat; on every beat player 1 offers a movement and player 2 offers one word of a story, while simultaneously each mirrors the other with a one-beat delay. Demanding split-attention exercise blending two related games.

Limitations scene game. Performers play a scene in a location that contains an enormous blob of blubber they must physically navigate around while never acknowledging that it exists. Tests scene focus and character consistency despite a distracting physical obstacle.

Concentration circle warm-up. Players pass a pattern around: each says 'Big Fish' (hands ~3 inches apart) to continue the direction, or 'Small Fish' (hands ~15 inches apart) to reverse direction. Mismatching the words and hand distance, or erring, earns a forfeit or a dramatic noisy exit. Any group size, no materials.

A Freeze Tag variation where, instead of players tagging in when ready, the MC calls 'Freeze' and calls in another player. Because players don't know when they'll be summoned they are less prepared and crazier, more exciting material results.

A listening-focused Harold variation: all performers sit with eyes closed (lights off if performed for an audience) and build the whole long form using only audio cues - dialogue, sound, and listening - with no visual contact. Primarily a listening exercise but has been staged as a long form.

Scene exercise for 3+. Players line up and get numbers; the instructor calls two numbers and those players take the stage immediately, each bringing a physical offer (an action like eating or cleaning) and a vocal offer (a line). They then accept and explore each other's offers to discover what the scene is about. More players give more number variety.

Musical performance game (a sung Pockets). Audience members write simple sentences on slips that go unread to players; during scenes a player draws a slip and must start a song beginning with that sentence, weaving it into the story. Any number of performers. Variation: leave slips on stage to be picked up during the show.
Musical performance game. The ensemble asks the audience for five things that make them feel down or troubled, then improvises a blues jam incorporating those five elements into the song.

Nonverbal telephone guessing game for four. Three players stand with ears covered and backs turned; the fourth gets a common expression and has one minute to convey it to player two using only mime and gibberish. Each player passes their understanding on to the next, then all reveal their interpretations to see how the message transformed.

Audience-participation performance game. Before the show, audience members write simple sentences on slips that go into a bucket. During a scene, at random moments players don't invent their next line but instead draw a slip and must use and justify that written line within the scene.

Name-learning concentration circle. Players learn their neighbors' names; the middle player points at someone and says 'bumpity bump bump bump', and that player must name their left and right neighbors before the phrase finishes or take the middle. Variation: the middle player can call the phrase to send everyone scrambling to new spots.

Scene-interruption game. Performers play a scene and at some point an onstage player gets a 'Call from Ray' (or any agreed name) - by phone, text, smoke signal, telepathy, etc.; Ray may never appear, and players improvise how the interruption changes the scene. Variation: replace it with a fixed line like 'I'll have a coke'.

Performance game (related to Actor's Nightmare). Two players each hold three cards bearing audience-written sentences; during the scene, instead of inventing a line they may play a card and must justify how that written phrase fits the conversation, blending scripted text with spontaneous scene work.

Musical performance game (related to Greatest Hits). One player is a CD-shop seller, another a customer; the audience names a gift recipient or occasion. The seller pitches several CDs, each with an explicit style/artist, and offers to demo a fitting song which other performers and a musician play; after 3-4 songs the buyer agrees to purchase and the scene ends.

Listening/observation exercise. Two performers improvise a scene making distinct strong physical and vocal character choices; once the audience clearly recognizes both characters, the players switch roles and replay the same scene with characters reversed. Pushes players beyond their default archetypes.

Energy warm-up. A caller names one of three couples - Knight and Queen, Prince and Princess, or Horse and Rider - and players pair up in the matching configuration (Queen on the kneeling Knight's knee; Prince carrying the Princess; Rider piggy-back on the standing Horse). The last pair to form it sits out a round; players mingle and seek new partners before the next call.

Rhythmic word-association warm-up. Players sit in a circle keeping a four-beat groove (slap thighs, clap, snap left, snap right) and throw a word to a neighbor on each right-hand snap. Works with free-association or Last-Letter rules. Variation: run two simultaneous circles with different rules, switching circles whenever you miss a beat.

Long-form format after David Mitchell's novel. In the first half the team tells several historical stories in different styles; after an intermission they finish them in reverse order, building thematic and object connections between the narratives. Works with any number of stories above two and any team size.

A competitive improv-comedy format resembling Theatresports. Two teams compete for audience-awarded points across roughly 7-12 short-form games drawn from a repertoire of 100+; a referee runs timing, calls fouls, and gathers audience suggestions. Signature penalty: the 'brown bag foul', a brown paper bag placed over an offending player's head.

Performance game. The audience names a product (real or invented) and players improvise an advertisement for it. Variations: play it as a radio commercial with the lights dimmed, or expand to the whole production process - marketing brainstorm, copywriting, jingle, and blooper reel from the shoot. Any number of performers.

Pairs physical warm-up. One player takes a position using their whole body; the partner completes it by folding over, in, or around them without touching, then they swap so the second player initiates a new pose. Advanced variation: each player adds one sentence of a story whenever they move to a new position, growing physical and narrative together.

A Freeze-Tag-style game where an observer steps in and repeats a line already spoken in the scene; the player who first said it leaves and a fresh scene begins from that repeated line. Variations: continue the existing scene instead of starting anew, replace all players rather than one, or call 'FLIP' to freeze before repeating a line. Builds associative thinking.

Limitations/performance game for two. Players run a scene; periodically one says 'What'd you say?' and the other must instantly replace their last line with a completely different phrase that rhymes with it, then play on. Players alternate stating lines and demanding rhyming replacements.
Two-player physical warm-up. In a chase, the player being pursued mimes obstacles for the chaser, who must physically overcome each imagined barrier. Builds object work and physical commitment.

Two-player spontaneity exercise. Each performer presents a personal crisis and an unrelated object; each must then instantly solve the other's crisis using only their own object. Replies must be instantaneous and may be ridiculous. Trains fast, creative problem-solving.

Icebreaker for 8+. Players sit in a circle; one in the center names something they have, have done, or can do, and everyone for whom it's true must cross the circle to a new spot, leaving one person in the center to pick the next prompt. Helps a new group find common ground.

Spontaneity exercise. A player picks an object in the room, starts by naming it, then deliberately makes sense of nothing - jumping rapidly between unrelated concepts and surreal images without dwelling on any single idea. Builds free, non-logical word association. Any number of players.

Performance game for four in two pairs. Two players perform a scene while the other two watch with ears covered, hearing nothing. The watchers then recreate the scene by copying the physical movements they saw while inventing entirely new dialogue. A limitations/replay exercise.

Group energy game. Everyone closes their eyes; one player is secretly the killer and one the retriever (marked by a towel/scarf). When the killer touches someone they scream and freeze; the retriever revives the dead by rubbing them with the towel. If the retriever is killed, the next living player to bump into them becomes the new retriever. Play till all are dead or bored.

Four-player monologue game (short-form cousin of Goon River). Players get audience-suggested identities/occupations, then over three rounds take turns describing the circumstances leading to their shared death, adding new information each round until all characters have died by round three. Weaves separate stories into one account. Also called Death Con.

Four players stand in a square; the MC gets audience suggestions for the front pair, who play a scene, then calls 'Right' or 'Left' to rotate the square so a new pair faces front. When players return to the front they continue their earlier scene, plainly or in a different time period. Also called Revolver, Pan Left Pan Right, or Turntable.

Character drill for two. Players run a scene; every time a bell rings, both must instantly switch into completely different characters while the scene continues. Unlikely to produce good scenes but excellent for teaching players to drop instantly into clear, varied characters.

Performance game. Players run a scene normally while a director (a non-performer or dedicated role) interrupts to 'cut' and redirect; the actors replay the scene with altered emotions, characters, or roles, like a film director coaching the cast. Explores how interpretations transform a scenario. Flexible group size.

Long form for large ensembles. The audience gives a disaster type and location; players stage classic disaster-movie scenes with archetypes (elderly couple, priest, eccentric scientist, fallen hero, child, troubled love interest). Disaster strikes (light, sound, and smoke effects encouraged), characters attempt survival and die off, and the hero, love interest, and surviving child escape safely.

Pairs concentration variant of Mirror. One player mirrors the partner but deliberately distorts the movements - exaggerating proportions (bigger, smaller, wider, narrower) or altering qualities like prettiness or ugliness - rather than reflecting accurately. Builds focus and imaginative physical interpretation.

Two-player exercise. In a set location, each player is secretly told something they must get the other to do, without the other knowing. They pursue their hidden goals through action and dialogue rather than instruction. Builds listening and risk-taking; audience laughter signals when a player is on the wrong track.

Two-player listening exercise. Both players simultaneously deliver a strong opening sentence, then work together to find the scene that makes sense of both. Variation: both react to each other's openings at the same time, then both react to those reactions simultaneously, heightening responsiveness.

Group warm-up. One player invents a name for a simple fictional children's game; on hearing it, everyone immediately starts playing it using only sounds and gibberish (no real language), trying to converge on the same rules without instruction. Variation: develop the game through play first, then name it afterward.

Long-form format mimicking a movie release. A narrator gives a trailer, then short scenes (max 5 lines each), then the cast of characters is presented, then the full movie is performed (with or without a director); afterward come 'special features' like deleted scenes and bloopers. A good bridge from short-form to long-form.

Two-part long form built on a chosen movie style. Part one: a collage of unrelated scenes typical of that genre, using 20-30 audience-given elements (character types, typical situations). After intermission the audience picks a favorite scene to replay with their help on details, and the cast performs the whole movie with that scene placed somewhere in the middle or end. Emphasizes how scenes connect into a larger narrative.

Concentration circle warm-up. A middle player points at others calling a gesture: elephant (trunk and ears), palm tree (trunk and swaying leaves), or car (steering wheel and wheels), and the targeted player plus neighbors must instantly form it with the right sound. When someone errs, add whatever they did to the list of options, growing the game until it overwhelms. Best with a large group.

Two-player emotion exercise requiring trust. One player opens with dialogue designed to shift the partner's emotional state up or down; the partner accepts and lets their character's emotion change accordingly. Variations: a solo version manipulating one's own character, or surprise statements like 'Honey I'm pregnant' to provoke authentic reactions. Targets characters, not the players themselves.

Four-player game. Two perform a scene while their partners are 'evil twins'; at any moment an evil twin calls 'freeze', tags in, and does something mischievous or destructive, then the original re-enters to justify the evil, repair the damage, and continue. Works well with setups like a first date or meeting the in-laws.

Energy warm-up. One player starts a small gesture (with or without a small sound); each player around the circle or line amplifies the movement and sound a bit more, the last taking it to the extreme. Players must stay faithful to the original gesture so it grows organically rather than becoming something new. Any group size.

Limitations scene game for 3+. Each player is assigned a secret word; two start a scene and the moment a waiting player hears their word they must justify leaving (or, for those onstage, exit). When that word is spoken again the player re-enters, all exits and entrances justified within the scene. Also called the Exit Game.

Long form for 3-5. Each player gets a random photo of a face they haven't seen; the audience supplies character details (name, motivations, desires, social background) and each introduces their character in a solo monologue. Following scenes put the characters in interaction, with assigned players staying in role while extras play supporting parts.

Group warm-up. The facilitator calls a theme ('Family of accountants', 'Family of pop stars') and players quickly build a physical portrait with their bodies, showing relationships and dynamics - who gets along, who's the outsider - through positioning alone. Requires close observation and nonverbal teamwork.

Endowment/performance game (an inverse of The Party) for 2+. One player gets a list of famous personalities, one per other player, and endows the others with those identities through behavior and dialogue, while they must recognize and embody the traits they're being given.

Long-form technique. When a character reveals an important detail about their past, the players quickly act out a series of brief chronological flashback scenes showing how that backstory developed, with fluent organic transitions, until enough is established to explain the present, then return to the main scene. Focuses on one character's past and avoids introducing other key characters.
An extension of Blind Freeze in which players add callbacks from earlier scenes, recycling characters and situations or even resuming scenes that were frozen before. A limitations/performance game.

Physical warm-up. Players form a pyramid (one at front, two behind, three behind them, etc.); the top player moves around the room and each row mimics the row directly ahead. Music can guide transitions; the top player may change direction or turn to face the second line. Variations: the top player interacts with the back row, or the formation reshapes as players collide.

Group concentration game. All but one player stand in a circle and secretly choose a leader; the middle player (who had eyes closed) opens them and tries to spot who is leading as the whole group copies the leader's clear, not-too-fast movements. The game ends once the leader is identified.

Long-form format. A scene runs with at least two characters; when one exits, the audience shouts 'follow the leaver' and all remaining performers leave the stage, the scene continuing with the character who just left in a totally new storyline. Players may take new roles in later scenes while the departing character stays consistent, producing a chain of linked-but-distinct scenes.

Physical warm-up. Players move around the space led by a body part the facilitator shouts, moving as though that part pulls them forward, cycling through parts and ending on a silly note by naming abstract things like internal organs. Also called Foot Soldiers.

Environment/object-work scene set in a hotel lobby, with one or more receptionists and others as guests, bell boys, or maintenance staff. Players build the environment together: once any player places a door, plant, or desk, everyone must respect it. Emphasizes collaborative world-building.

Long-form/character game. One performer lies 'deceased' on a table while the audience suggests an unusual cause of death, which is briefly enacted; then players approach as funeral guests and deliver monologues about their relationship with the deceased, each acted out as a flashback. Any number of performers.

Line-up performance game for Theatresports. Players form two facing lines; the MC calls a word or title and the next player in line gets 30 seconds to do their thing based on the suggestion, after which a new prompt cues the next performer. High-energy, trains quick thinking. Any number that can form two lines.

Performance game (like invent-your-own-game). The performers ask the audience to name a non-existent improv game, then make up and announce its rules on the spot and play it. Best for groups experienced in short-form, who can invent rules easily.
Mental-flexibility/gibberish warm-up. Players walk around the room pointing at objects and renaming each with made-up nonsense words ('Jabbertalk'). Any number of players. Related to Malapropism.

Fast reaction drill. One player is the 'goalie'; the others prepare opening lines and characters and rapidly bombard the goalie with offers one at a time. The goalie must react immediately to each offer, acknowledge the opening and character, snap into an opposite character, and reply, before the next player fires. Trains instinctive character work without overthinking.

Advanced format (Keith Johnstone) for three experienced players: two act scenes while the third directs, rotating who directs. The audience votes by yelling 'Banana' for a good scene or 'Die'/'Forfeit' for a bad one, and directors earn bananas based on approval. The director with the most bananas wins. Uniquely rewards directing over acting, lowering inter-player competition.

Four-player game. Two players are 'Ground Controllers' who use flashlights with cone attachments to direct two performers' physical movement; the performers cannot move unless directed, and all movement must be justified within the scene. The light's position sets direction and height, prompting walking, climbing, or crawling. Variation: audience members operate the flashlights.

Object-work group exercise. One player enters a mimed space through a door and exits; each subsequent player enters the established space, adding mimed objects or new doors while respecting everything placed before, until everyone has gone. Players must avoid 'gagging' - adding incongruous elements (a jukebox in a clearly-defined church) that break coherence.

Narration/performance game. One player arrives as a guest at a location (e.g. ringing a doorbell to pick up a date) while the other performers act suspiciously, dropping clues to a hidden secret through strange behavior. The scene ends when the audience discovers the secret, which can be dark or lighthearted. Any number of performers.

Performance game for 5+. The group gets four audience suggestions and turns them into characters: two superheroes (a main hero and a sidekick) and two villains (a main villain and an aide), with the rest as victims. Heroes and villains weave as many of their assigned attributes into the scene as possible.

Limitations/performance game. The audience suggests a well-known fairy tale and a specific handicap or peculiar mental state for each character; players improvise the story embodying those constraints. Described as very silly but very effective.

Trust exercise for 16+. All players but one form two facing lines and link hands to make a platform, then heave the last player along from one end of the line to the other. Players should remove shoes, coins, and loose items first for safety.

Endowment/guessing game for four. One player leaves while the others pick a mode of transport, an object, and a goal. The player returns and must deduce the transport, then use the object to hijack the others and accomplish the goal, with the others giving only action-based hints. Also called Rebel without a Clue; related to Who Where Why Am I.

Two-player musical game. Players take turns singing four-line compliments about each other, the fourth line always 'I love you'. After both sing their verses they repeat the lines in an interwoven, alternating pattern and finish together on 'I love you'. May rhyme but doesn't have to.

Two-player character exercise. The customer enters a shop with a character built from a suggestion (a voice, facial expression, body part, emotion, or frozen position); the shopkeeper must imitate the customer's character traits as closely as possible while a simple shop transaction plays out. Trains character creation for the customer and listening/watching for the shopkeeper. Counterpart to Opposite Characters.

Competitive short-form format: 2-4 teams of 2 players perform rounds of improvised scenes on referee-given themes (which may impose restrictions like silence or a specific style), with five seconds of prep per scene, and the audience votes the winning team. Teams wear elaborate wrestling-style costumes (any dress-up goes).
