Competitive format popular in French-speaking countries: two teams of six (three men, three women) play three 30-minute rounds like an ice-hockey match. A referee draws challenges specifying title, player count, category (e.g. Science Fiction, Musical) and duration; players improvise while the ref whistles faults (dragging, off-theme, blocking). Three faults gives the opponents a point; the audience votes on disputed calls and throws slippers to show disapproval.

Three-player game. One player is an expert on an audience topic, another the interviewer, and the third a sign-language interpreter who provides simultaneous 'interpretation for the deaf'. Works best slow to allow translation; gets funnier when the interpreter literally signs every word, including fillers like 'oh' and 'great'.

Performance game for 2+. One character is invisible to the audience while the other performers act as though that unseen character is present and visible, interacting through dialogue and physical reaction to create the illusion. Variation: an off-stage performer voices the invisible character.

Physical/character warm-up. Players move around the room until the trainer calls 'Yes!', when everyone jumps into a frozen position; the trainer may add a quality (horizontal, up, down, big, small, light, heavy). Players then use their resulting pose to inspire a character or situation through free association. Extended variation: Association Jump.

High-energy circle game based on Bunny. The middle bunny may raise hands overhead, lunge left or right, and 'eat one of her own ears', eliminating that neighbor - but any player who shouts 'Die' while the bunny's arms are raised eliminates the bunny instead. Combines quick reactions with silly comedy.

Circle elimination warm-up. Each player picks an animal with a motion and sound; a player 'sends' by doing their own animal's noise and motion then another player's, who responds with their own and passes on. Players are eliminated for mistakes until one remains. The sillier the animals, the better.

Concentration warm-up. Four to six players stand at the corners of the playing area with one in the middle; two corner players make eye contact and try to swap corners while the middle player races to steal an empty corner. Play fast; harder with diagonal eye contacts than adjacent ones.

Narration game. Players perform a scene, then replay it several times from different characters' perspectives; requires clear relationships and conflicting viewpoints (transactional scenes work poorly). Expansion: one performer tells a story while others narrate the same events from alternate viewpoints. Also called Rashomon or Kurosawa.

Coordination circle warm-up. Players pass things to neighbors with distinct gestures: first names, then the alphabet A-Z with another gesture, then numbers 1-9 with another; once each is mastered, all three are passed simultaneously. Variation: substitute months of the year or musical notes, each with its own gesture.

Silent ensemble-agreement exercise. All players move around the room together until they collectively sense and agree on a shared reason to exit; everyone must leave at the same time and the reason should be obvious to all. No speaking. Any group size.

Two-player narrative exercise. After establishing a location, one player pitches story offers ('let's find a talking crab') and the other accepts or rejects each; rejected offers prompt new pitches. Trains players to recognize strong story directions and to drop their own ideas for better ones.

Performance game. One player acts out a scene while others voice inanimate objects or creatures in the environment (a talking ant in a forest, a toothbrush in a bathroom), making immediately clear what is speaking. Variation: script the object lines in advance and have the main actor justify them, like Actor's Nightmare.

Long form built around a single fixed setting (e.g. a post office). Characters wander in and out and time shifts and playbacks are allowed, but the environment never changes location for the whole performance. Trains scene-building within a spatial constraint.

Supportive warm-up. Players throw a ball, preferably naming the catcher, who deliberately fails to catch it; rather than mocking the miss, the group cheers genuine praise ('Good move!', 'Great energy!'), celebrating mistakes and building a fearless atmosphere. Any group size.

Long-form format. Players start from one audience suggestion and play a scene; any performer can interrupt with 'This reminds me of...' to introduce an associative link that launches a new scene, chaining scenes together through free association.

Status performance game. One player is the Master planning something (e.g. a party) and giving instructions to servants seated in a line; whenever the Master looks away, the servants pull exaggerated faces behind their back, and any servant caught is dismissed and replaced. Best with bold risk-taking servants and a strict, merciless Master.

Association warm-up for 2+. Players walk around the room, point at any object, and give it another (wrong) name. Demonstrates that association is a natural skill; especially helpful for performers who think they 'can't associate'.

Elimination energy warm-up. Players spread in a staggered line and the caller gives commands with set physical responses: 'Land ahoy' (hop on one foot saluting), 'Hit the deck' (push-up position), 'octopus' (stacked push-up pairs), 'Man overboard' (piggyback pairs), 'two three four' (sit and row). The last to complete each action is eliminated until one remains. Any group size.

Endowment/guessing game for 4+ (therapist, a couple, and a host). One player is sent out while the host gets two relationship problems from the audience; the couple portrays both problems and the returning therapist must diagnose them through questioning and interaction, succeeding once both issues are identified.

Long form usually for two players seated in chairs who take turns speaking in character about their pasts; a series of scenes follows, with the chairs moved for each new location and their exact positions recreated when returning to a previous location. The show ends when the chairs return to their original front-stage spot and the story resolves. Allows more than two players.

Trust/icebreaker warm-up. Players stand in a circle and massage the shoulders of their right-hand neighbor for about a minute, then reverse direction. Variation: pair up and massage each other's temples, calves, or other appropriate areas depending on group comfort.

Two-player justification exercise. The servant refuses each of the master's requests and explains why it's impossible, with escalating explanations that interlock; the master accepts each refusal and asks for something else, until it's revealed that all the servant's answers connect to a single unfolding disaster.

Competitive elimination format (Keith Johnstone) for up to ~20 players with 2 directors. Player names sit on a scoreboard; directors pick performers for each scene, and the audience awards points by cheering/applause, all players in a scene scoring equally. Starts with big group games and shrinks to smaller scenes as low scorers are eliminated each round. Good for mixed-skill groups. Also spelled Maestro.

Group energy warm-up. Players stand in a circle with linked arms, move to a wall and squash into two parallel facing lines, then the whole formation wheels along the walls of the room at high speed. Keep hands open (not fisted) and avoid collisions; needs a clear, wall-lined space.

Status exercise. Everyone plays geese and establishes a pecking order through nonverbal clucking and interaction, with one Mother Goose at the top; each player should sense who is just above them. The group then tries to line up in the correct pecking order they've created.

Character drill (institutionalized 'pimping'). Players call out trait-based character names ('Mr. Bad Irish Accent', 'Mrs. Pathological Liar') and the named player must instantly improvise that extravagant character. Mainly a rehearsal tool but usable in performance.

Musical narration game for 5-7 performers plus a musician. The facilitator assigns each player a musical style and gets an audience member's favorite childhood fairy tale; players take turns singing the tale in their own styles, each advancing the plot from where the last left off until the story ends.

Energy/risk warm-up. Players walk around while two hold water-filled plastic bottles; on eye contact a holder throws the bottle, and if it's dropped both thrower and receiver lie down and shout 'My Fault' as loud as possible before playing on. Variations: treat the bottle as red-hot or change its imagined weight. Any group size.

Listening/cooperation exercise for 2-4. Players collaboratively describe an unknown object none of them has predetermined, each offering one non-noun descriptive in turn, building toward a single coherent item until it becomes obvious what the object is (or they get stuck).

Pairs word-at-a-time exercise. Two players build a scene in a chosen location where they meet a creature, give it a name, and flee; the 'monster' can be anything (an evil witch, a dragon, a frog with a machine gun, a smelly French cheese). Variations: fight, befriend, or ride the monster instead of running. Teaches improvisers to explicitly name the problem in a scene.

Monologue game. A single object sits on a chair on stage; three performers in turn deliver individual monologues as different characters inspired by that object, each new character logically connected to and justified by the previous ones through the shared object. Challenges players to make distinct, unpredictable yet connected characters.

Two-player scene exercise. Each performer gets a current job and a former job; rather than directly playing the old job, they fold its character traits and mannerisms into how they do the new one, mining comedy from the contrast between past and present occupations.

Joke-construction line-up game (related to World's Worst and Sex With Me Is Like). A term is announced ('elephants') and players deliver a three-line joke: '185 [term] walk into a bar', the bartender's refusal to serve them, and a witty punchline reply. Emphasizes wordplay and quick wit rather than scene work.

An MC interviews a group of players who collectively portray a single character, all speaking simultaneously to answer each question so it sounds like one character with many mouths. Answers should make grammatical sense and be clear; works best with obvious, simple answers at a measured pace, each player both leading and following. Adaptable as an audience warm-up.

Platform-building exercise. One player opens a scene with a deliberately incomplete, vague offer that doesn't yet define who/what/where; a second player enters and finishes establishing the basic circumstances. Teaches the ensemble to build the platform together rather than one person defining everything.

exercise_name: Word at a Time Expert (Two-headed Professor / Oracle)
description: Three-player game. An interviewer questions two performers who together play a single expert on an audience topic, delivering answers one word at a time per player. Variations: 'Two-headed Professor' and 'Oracle' (an ancient Greek oracle answering questions about life and love). The interviewer can escalate by asking the expert to sing instead of answer.

Four-player listening drill. A central player must simultaneously answer arithmetic questions from the left player, personal questions from the right player, and mirror the movements of the player in front; any neglected player repeats 'Beep beep beep' until served. Players rotate positions every few minutes. Trains split attention and listening.

Line-up heightening game. The first player names an object and its function ('I'm a paperclip, and I hold loose papers together'); the next adds a related object with a similar function, establishing a pattern, and successive players heighten it with increasingly creative or absurd examples that keep the core relationship. At peak heightening a new round starts with a fresh object.

Performance game. The audience gives two locations; two pairs of performers simultaneously play separate scenes in their own environments on the same stage, each pair ignoring characters and events from the other scene. Needs careful facilitation so both pairs get enough time. Trains focus.

Concentration circle warm-up. Players pass the word 'Yes' to their left-hand neighbor around the circle; any player can say 'No' to reverse direction to the right. Goal is to pass 'Yes' around as fast as possible. Once mastered, repeat with eyes closed for an added concentration challenge.

Association circle warm-up. Players take turns saying words that build on the cumulative theme of all prior words rather than just associating off the last one (e.g. grass, plant, flower, tree, forest, jungle), heightening the pattern as a group; restart when the theme can no longer escalate.

Object-work concentration warm-up. Players mill about, each miming a particular kind of ball with specific weight or texture; at the trainer's sign everyone passes their ball to someone else, repeated several times, after which everyone tries to find their own original ball among the group. Builds object work and focus.

exercise_name: Word at a Time Scene (Ping Pong)
description: Two players build a whole scene speaking one word at a time in alternation, first establishing location/identity then physically enacting (not just describing) the story - 'Play it, don't say it' - often with a director cutting scenes. Variation: a third player adds a second character with a distinct voice/accent for comic chaos ('Ping Pong'), prioritizing humor over coherence.

Two-player audience-participation game. Beforehand the audience writes simple sentences on slips; each performer draws three unread and puts them in their pocket. During the scene a player can replace their next line by drawing a slip and incorporating/justifying whatever line they find into the scene as their own words.

Group energy warm-up. Players squat as 'corn' while the instructor narrates a heating pan; as it gets hotter players 'pop' by jumping up, clapping overhead, and saying 'pop', starting gradually, building as a group, then dying down. Variation: 'char' the popcorn by forgetting to take the pan off the heat for a funny ending.

Musical long form needing a versatile musician (same as Song Style Galore). The audience gives ~10 song styles and a story; players perform the story straight while the musician weaves all the requested styles throughout. Also called Song Style Galore.

Pairs acceptance/association warm-up. One player offers an imaginary present with open hands (not predetermined) and the partner names it with the first thing that comes to mind ('a little dead bird'); they swap roles, the receiver immediately passing back a different gift. Play fast to avoid overthinking, and celebrate every present whatever it is.

Vocal energy circle warm-up. One player steps forward, makes a bold gesture and a loud sound; everyone copies both, then the next player takes a turn. Emphasizes open, amplified vocalization - yelling en masse is good for the soul. Any number of players.

Object-association performance game. Performers get an object and must demonstrate an unconventional use for it (not its intended purpose), drawing on its physical features or parts - e.g. a chair becomes the bars of a prison cell. Players take turns showcasing imaginative interpretations. Popularized by Whose Line Is It Anyway?

Long-form format (La Carpe Haute) needing a musician, DJ, or music source. A series of scenes connected by music, each inspired by a well-known song with the music treated as part of the scene's environment; characters transition to a new scene by starting a new song (e.g. turning on a radio), and scenes end when characters leave the music's location or are interrupted.

Environment/object-work scene. One player is a broker showing a second player (or several) around an audience-given space; players may create any objects but may not ask questions, every object must be justified by someone, and once placed objects stay put unless explicitly moved.

Endowment/guessing game. One player leaves while the audience picks an object and a non-obvious problem with it; the player returns as a repair-shop customer/worker and must discover the issue through interaction, winning once identified. Variations: the shopkeeper gives hints; a malfunctioning animal ('Veterinarian Endowment'); or reverse it so the shopkeeper guesses.

Listening drill. In a dialogue, before adding their own new line each player must first repeat the entire dialogue spoken by the previous player (excluding the repetitions that player already made). A training tool, not a performance piece, for active listening.

Two-player exercise. Players perform a short (~1 minute) scene, then immediately replay the identical scene using only gibberish, preserving the physical comedy, emotional beats, and narrative through vocal expression alone. Builds gibberish ('Jabbertalk') skill and shows how much communicates without real words.

Verbal-wit performance game. The audience gives a statement or fact and players must invent a witty question for which it is the answer (e.g. 'Green Bananas' -> 'What is best avoided if you have constipation?'). Prizes verbal creativity and humor over scene work.

Performance game. The audience gives an everyday activity and players perform it as if it were a ritual, heightening the ceremony with frameworks like religious tradition, sports protocol, or formal government procedure so the mundane becomes solemn and meaningful. One or more players.

Two-player mirroring exercise. Partners set a steady beat; player 1 makes a new movement on every beat and player 2 mirrors it with a one-beat delay. Increase difficulty with 2- or 3-beat delays. Extended version: Bidirectional Satellite TV.

Performance/musical game. Players perform a wordless scene in which the characters' emotions are controlled by the music, shifting as the soundtrack shifts. Builds emotional responsiveness and physical expression.

Group physical exercise for an even number. Players form two circles - an inner 'clay' circle facing out and an outer 'sculptor' circle facing in; each sculptor molds their player into a pose then rotates clockwise to the next, and after a full rotation back to their original piece, sculptors name and introduce their creations. Variation: a 'voice chip' lets each statue speak one sentence when activated.

Elimination circle warm-up. Players are cowboys; when the facilitator calls a name, that player drops to the floor and their two neighbors 'shoot' each other - whoever is slower to drop, or fires after someone already dropped, is eliminated. Continues until two remain for a back-to-back Western duel. Prizes chivalry and accepting elimination cheerfully. Variations: spin 360 before firing, or walk around the space.

Limitations performance game. Players perform a scene with the spatial orientation flipped - the back wall is treated as the floor and the floor as a wall - creating gravity-defying actions and choices like hanging upside down. For a small group.

Four-player endowment game. Each player secretly assigns one of three traits - sexy, silly, or stinky - to each other player; the group then plays a scene at a social gathering (party, picnic) and afterward the audience guesses which player got which endowment from their performance choices.

Concentration warm-up. One player is Simon and gives commands; players must only obey those prefixed with 'Simon says', and anyone who follows an unprefixed command is out. Simon tries to trick players into automatic responses (e.g. nodding when asked if they understand). Builds attention and self-control; tricked-out players can sometimes re-enter.

Three-player limitations scene: at all times one player must be standing, one sitting, and one lying down, so whenever one changes position another must immediately adjust, with the moves justified in the story. Variation 'Glad Sad Mad' applies the same rule to three emotional states instead of positions.

Group storytelling/time-pressure game. Players get one minute to plan how to complete an assigned task (launch a product, build a clubhouse) across six separate scenes, then must immediately perform all six with no further discussion. Rewards fast agreement and acceptance - quarreling only wastes time.

Pairs word-association warm-up. Partners trade associated words; if a player hesitates, says 'Erm', or is too slow, the other gives a gentle slap on the face. The mild consequence pushes faster, more spontaneous association and breaks the fear of saying whatever comes to mind.

An improvised soap-opera episode with several storylines running at once, each advancing in tiny steps; playable long- or short-form. Encourages parody of soap tropes - melodramatic acting, surprise relationship reveals, and classic settings like hospitals or offices. For an ensemble cast.

Solo character exercise. One performer enters as a character through a door (the door type establishing the environment), then addresses themselves as a different character in the same space, with one character eventually exiting through a door; players cycle through multiple characters fairly fast to explore their range and build a platform. Solo version of Doors.

Endowment/guessing game for five. One player is the bride and leaves; the other four each get an audience item representing 'something old', 'something new', 'something borrowed', and 'something blue'. The bride returns and must identify each item from the players' hints, who can't say what they have directly and ideally reference one another's items.

Performance/musical game. Players run a scene that can be interrupted at any moment by someone declaring 'Sounds like a song', whereupon the performers must spontaneously sing a number inspired by the last line spoken or last action done, then return to the scene. Blends dialogue scenes with song.

Performance technique/game. More than one scene runs in parallel and performers organically move the audience's focus from one scene to another and back; transferring focus to a new scene without returning creates an 'Organic Edit'. Usable standalone or as a long-form tool.

Silly performance game. Two players run a scene each holding a glass of water; players take a spit after their own line, after the other's line, or both, mining comedy from the timing of spitting water during the dialogue.

Long-form narration format: a single storyline that runs straight forward in time with no flashbacks or subplots, the cast collaboratively developing one linear arc from beginning to end. The base structure for many sung and themed long forms (e.g. Standard Musical).

Solo character exercise. One performer tells a story to an audience of empty chairs while progressively embodying all its characters, narrating between portrayals and choosing storylines that naturally establish distinct character traits (e.g. opening 'Jodi didn't really like leaving the house' to set up agoraphobia). Emphasizes character and physical storytelling over plot.

Performance game. Two players run a scene; whenever a performer needs to do something physically challenging or emotionally uncomfortable, a third player enters as their stunt double to perform that action, then freezes and steps back so the original actor resumes.

Group trust exercise. Players split into two equal teams; one team closes their eyes as 'clay' while the 'sculptors' use open-hand touch to mold them into a connected sculpture. The sculptors then become clay and recreate the statue from memory with eyes closed, and the original clay players (eyes closed) try to identify themselves in the imitation before discussing its accuracy.

Solo long-form format (Andy Eninger; named after the multiple-personality case study). One performer plays all characters and their dialogue, alternating between scenes and monologues (internal or addressed to the audience) that build narrative and character. Requires a single performer.

Musical long form set in a band's rehearsal room. Players establish the band's name, members, and album title (often from audience suggestions), then rehearse every song on their playlist while developing character dynamics and relationships (romantic or conflicted song inspirations) that evolve through the session.

Solo performance exercise. One player improvises nonstop for 10 minutes, opening with a character monologue of up to 60 seconds, then two-character scenes featuring that character, using transitions to spin off new characters and situations throughout. Goals: never stop, and generate as many distinct characters and scenarios as possible.

Performance game. One player tells a silly, absurd story to the audience while trying to keep a straight face; the moment the audience laughs, that player is replaced by another who gets a fresh shot. Players take turns trying to deliver the ridiculous narrative without triggering laughter.

exercise_name: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly Advice
description: Line-up wit game for three. The audience submits questions or problems and each of the three players gives progressively worse counsel - good, then bad, then 'ugly' - with an MC assigning roles for variety. As an elimination game, any player whose worse advice isn't topped by an even worse one is replaced.

Pairs concentration/trust exercise. One player holds a still 'sculpture' pose while the partner, eyes closed, explores the statue's form by touch, then attempts to physically replicate the exact posture from memory. Builds focus and kinesthetic awareness. Related to Swedish Sculptors.

Two-player look-and-listen exercise. One player initiates and speaks a first line; the second repeats it verbatim. The group pauses to discuss everything established nonverbally and in the line, ensuring both fully absorbed it, then restarts the scene to develop naturally. Builds observation and listening.

Competitive improv format (Keith Johnstone). Two teams compete across a series of improv games judged by a panel; an MC runs a warm-up, introduces the judges and teams, and the audience helps decide winners by cheering, awarding five points to the victor. Features scene time limits, a horn to warn against boring content, and basket-head penalties. Danish variant uses a single judge ('Ombuds') and is friendlier for beginners.

Performance game. The cast plays a continuous scene that advances through historical eras, from prehistoric times to the future, keeping the same storyline but adapting characteristics and attributes appropriate to each 'time', with each leap justified and advancing the narrative. Unlimited players.

Limitations scene game. Performers may only speak while physically touching another player, so they're pushed to explore varied contact - hugging, fighting, tickling - rather than dull shoulder taps. Works best in settings where touching is unexpected, like a confession booth or sauna. Related to Move and Speak.

Long-form performance game (Forrest Brakeman, 1989; licensed). Improvisers create three separate plays from three audience suggestions, structured in three rounds: all three first acts, then all three second acts, then all three finales. Some perform each play in a different style (Shakespeare, Western, musical).

Line-up wit game. The MC reads Trivial Pursuit questions (audience-chosen categories) to a line of players, each inventing the funniest possible answer rather than the correct one; the MC screens out questions with a single obvious answer in favor of vague ones. Variation: the MC reads an answer and players invent the question.

Performance game for three: a lead anchor, a weather presenter, and a reporter on location improvise a TV newscast together, inventing content on the spot. Variation: take an audience suggestion for a central theme tying the broadcast together.

Pairs concentration/observation warm-up. One player studies their partner's appearance, then closes their eyes while the partner makes three changes to how they look; on reopening, the observer must identify what has changed. Builds attention to detail and visual awareness.

Association exercise. One player stands before the group while the others imagine what they'd be as a car, flower, building, era, foreign country, mineral, beverage, etc., sharing the metaphors aloud with no wrong answers. Reveals how others perceive someone; repeating over time shows how familiarity shifts the responses. Any group size.

Concentration circle warm-up. Players pass phrases in alternating directions: clockwise 'Whisky Mixer', counterclockwise 'Mister Whisker', and any player can reverse with 'Misty Vista'. Tongue-twisting by design; if anyone smiles or laughs they must run a lap around the circle, while others try to crack them up.

Name-learning rhythm game. The group chants 'Who stole the cookies from the cookie jar?'; the player who is 'it' accuses another by name, who denies it ('Couldn't be!') and names someone else, continuing the call-and-response cycle. Helps a group learn names. Any group size.

Limitations scene game. Performers play a scene with no dialogue, but may use environmental sounds (slamming doors, running water, birdsong, echoing footsteps), relying on physicality, expression, and body language to carry the story. Related to (and inverts) Without Sound.

Musical version of Word at a Time Scene. Players collaboratively create a song contributing one word at a time, sung to a known melody (easier) or to a tune played on piano (the musician should not play too fast). Combines lyrical improvisation with melodic constraint.

Limitations performance game. Two players perform a scripted firing scene keeping the exact dialogue but adding physical comedy, mime, and expression. Round two: a director secretly side-coaches one player (be nervous, add a physical quirk, change emotion) without the other knowing. Shows how much players can do without deviating from a script.

Performance game. Players run a scene; at any time the host calls 'zoom-out' and the action shifts to tiny 'finger puppet' scale to simulate distance, or 'zoom-in' to return to normal size, switching as desired. Builds adaptability and physical comedy through rapid scale shifts. Any number of performers.

Performance game for four. Each performer picks a distinct TV format (news broadcast, documentary, cartoon, etc.); the audience gives a central theme and an MC 'zaps' between the four channels, each of which must incorporate the same theme, for comedy from the clash of formats.

Solo storytelling exercise. One player narrates a story while three others tag in to demand specific elements: more action/narrative, environmental detail (color), or emotional depth. Trains improvisers to build richer, more dimensional stories balancing plot with sensory detail and feeling.

Long-form format that opens with an audience interview: one audience member names a location of emotional significance and is interviewed in depth about its layout, memories, and secrets; a series of scenes then plays out, all connected to that information, set in the place or inspired by its revelations. Needs several performers.

A Harold-based long form where all scenes happen in the same motel room. Players run three storylines across three beats, with monologues between beats revealing secrets other characters don't know; scenes may share or differ in time period, concluding with a third beat for each storyline.

Trust exercise for 3+. One player runs across a wide space with eyes closed while the others stand along the side edges to keep them from drifting too far left or right and to catch them at the end. Runners often start sensing an imaginary wall ahead though the space is clear. Builds spatial trust.

Tongue-twister counting circle (a Buzz/Fizz variant). Players count around saying 'smart fellas, they felt smart', but for any number containing 3 or divisible by 3 they say 'smart fellas, they all felt smart'. Misstate the phrase and you're eliminated; the repeated phrases get harder to say as the count rises.

Physical warm-up. Group members take turns demonstrating a stretch of a body part which everyone copies, repeating until the whole body is stretched. Humorous variation: stretch fictional or impossible body parts like eyeballs, ears, or hair. No equipment; any group size.

Performance game. Players run a scene whose length is set by an external timing mechanism rather than a clock - e.g. how long a player can hold their head underwater in a bucket, or how long it takes the audience to throw 20 socks on stage, or to finish a drink. The scene runs until that event concludes. Any number of performers.

Coordination physical warm-up. Four numbered gestures - forehead touch, shoulder touch, hip touch, foot lift - are built up progressively: call 'one-two-three-four' twice, then combine gestures with countdown calls (each stage done twice), finishing by running all gestures in sequence at increasing speed. No minimum player count.

Movement-imitation warm-up. Players form a line; the first walks a big circle around the room and the second follows, mimicking their movements. After several rounds the leader goes to the back and the next player mimics the new leader. Emphasizes natural observation rather than exaggerated or comedic moves.

Focus warm-up. Players stand in a circle, numbered sequentially, keeping an arm rhythm; on each beat the active player calls another player's number, who must call a different number on the next beat. Anyone who fails or breaks the rhythm moves to the last position and all numbers shift accordingly.

Pairs concentration warm-up. Partners keep a thigh-slap beat and on each beat pick one of four hand moves (both up, point left, point right, point down); when they happen to match the same direction, on the next slap both point hands at each other miming a gun and say 'psssst', then reset.

Energy circle warm-up. Players in turn say 'Ha', 'Soh', 'Kah' while pointing to the next player with hands at different heights (forehead, chin, both hands). On a mistake the group rhythmically chants 'You are out of this game' and that player steps out to try to disrupt the remaining circle. A warm-up and a lesson in handling failure.

Object-work circle warm-up. Players walk around throwing pantomimed objects, establishing eye contact before each throw: first a knife thrown ninja-style, then a carefully thrown baby with its own sound, then an angry cat with its own vocalization, adding more objects each with a distinct throwing style and sound.

Endowment/guessing game (a generalized Hijacker). One player is a crime-ring leader meeting others to plan or pull off a crime, secretly endowed with three things - something to steal/hijack/kill, a method or weapon, and a wild card (a code word or disguise) - which they must deduce from the others' behavior as the scene unfolds.

Pairs emotion drill. Players face a partner, arms relaxed, and silently portray assigned emotions (pity, lust, joy) using no hands or sounds, then rotate partners and repeat. The facilitator yells an emotion and players must find the partner they did it with and redo it; advanced, players roam and show the right emotion on meeting each of their three partners, neutral in between. Vary the emotions.
Very silly two-player performance game. Players run a scene and every time one makes the audience laugh, the other slaps them. Purely for comic effect.

Concentration circle warm-up. Players stand in a circle; one makes eye contact with another and the two clap simultaneously, then the receiver makes eye contact with a new player to clap together, continuing the pattern and speeding up once the rhythm settles. Energizes a group.

Two-player musical game in four beats. Each player picks an occupation; first each sings (on their own melody) about their job's upsides while naming one thing they lack; they meet in a bar and state their problem in one line each; finally a duet on a third melody resolves both problems by trading what one has in excess for what the other needs.

Trust exercise for ~8. Players split into two facing lines and interlock forearms to form a human platform, then launch another player into the air and catch them on descent. The platform stays sturdy by holding each other at the wrists. Builds ensemble trust.

Competitive concentration circle (a Big Booty relative). Players get numbers and pass calls in a four-beat rhythm to the tune 'Big Brother, Big Brother'; whoever fails to respond to their called number moves to the lowest spot beside Big Brother and all numbers shift. Needs practiced timing, 3+ players. Variant: Boom She Boom.

Group movement warm-up. Players mill in Brownian motion, then raise their left hand to rest on someone's left shoulder (one hand per shoulder); once bonded the hand-shoulder connection must not break, forming molecular clusters that move together. Variations: use both hands, use ankles instead of shoulders, or change energy and add sound effects.

Listening/synchronization circle. Pairs step forward, each says 'I have a word', then count down and simultaneously say the word they're thinking of; success is when both say the identical word, achieved by making small conceptual steps rather than chasing laughs. Variations: a Two Hander pairs version, and an Elimination version where non-matching players sit out.

Concentration circle warm-up (a Big Fish Small Fish variant). Players pass imaginary fish calling 'big fish' or 'small fish' while sizing them with their hands; the receiver accepts at the matching size and must alternate when passing on. Repeat a size, mismatch words and hands, or err and the group calls 'Fish Story' and that player casts across the circle to restart. Add other sea creatures or make it an elimination game.

Nonverbal teamwork warm-up. Players line up facing one way; the leader calls a characteristic (height, shoe size, hair color) and the group must silently reorganize itself in that order, committing confidently - collective decisiveness matters more than accuracy. Can be done eyes-closed with spotters; harder with personal traits or combined criteria. Any number.

Cumulative-memory circle warm-up. The first player describes and mimes an action for 'Leslie'; everyone repeats the words and mime. Each next player adds a new action while the group recites and mimes all previous ones in sequence, growing the chain around the circle. Variations: speed up, require the actions to rhyme, or go cross-circle instead of in order.

Concentration circle game. Players form a tight circle looking down; on a count of three everyone looks up, choosing to look left, right, or across, and when two players lock eyes they both briefly scream and look back down. Elimination variant: locked-eye pairs step out and the circle closes. Variations: laugh or sing an agreed note instead of screaming.

Acceptance circle warm-up. One player mimes a simple activity; another jumps in saying 'Let me help you!', and the mime replies 'Thank you, I am [radically different activity]ing', which the helper then mimes - and so on until everyone has gone. Trains players to instantly drop their assumption about what's happening. Variation 'Copying' has the helper gracefully transition between the old and new activity.

Silly tag-style warm-up. Players mill about, each secretly an 'egg' or a 'sperm', and secretly pick one player as a barrier and one gamete to chase or avoid; if a sperm catches its egg they hug, both are out, then join hands and float joyfully among the chaos. Emphasizes listening, acceptance, and silliness over winning. Best with 4-5+ players. Related variation: Body Guard.

Elimination energy warm-up (a pirate-themed Man Overboard). Players form a line and respond to pirate commands with set physical actions, each needing a set number of players combined: 'AHOY!' (stand on one leg and salute), 'OCTOPUS!' (two players make a wiggling eight-limbed creature), 'WALK THE PLANK!' (hop with bound hands and ankles), 'BURY THE TREASURE!' (mime digging). The leader can invent new commands. Any group size.

Exaggeration circle warm-up. The first player makes a subtle, unconventional pose and sound which the next player repeats but enlarges, growing louder and bigger each pass across the circle; when it can't enlarge further the leader calls 'stop' and starts fresh. Needs 4-5+ players. Variation: Exaggeration Circle (same rules without crossing the circle).

Trust exercise. One player walks slowly with eyes closed around a circle of spotters (need more than four) who silently redirect them toward the center with gentle shoulder touches when they near the edge; emphasizes consent and comfort. Advanced: the walker makes distracting noises; gimmick: the circle moves so the walker can't learn its position. Also called Walkies.

Rhythm concentration circle. Players pass 'tick' and 'tock' left or right by pointing; any player can interrupt with 'o'clock', point across, and name a time (e.g. '4 o'clock'), and the pointed player must say 'bong' that many times before resuming the tick-tock. Variations: 'Military Clock' (24-hour time) and 'Time Dilation' (change the pace). Any group size.

Mime-justification circle warm-up (a What Are You Doing relative). One player mimes a simple action (e.g. brushing teeth) then boldly tells the next player they're doing something else while keeping the same mime; each player repeats the identical mime with a new justification. It always ends in failure as justifications run out - the point is to fail with grace and laughter. Variation: play in lines or pairs, or change the mime object each time.

Trust warm-up. Players mill with eyes closed while wall spotters gently redirect them to the center; one player is the vampire, and when they grab another's wrist that player screams, opens their eyes, and becomes a spotter, until everyone has been 'eaten'. Variation: Zombie Walk uses a zombie instead.

Trust warm-up for any size group. Players mill with eyes closed while stationed spotters keep them safe; 'patient zero' infects others by grabbing a wrist, making them cry 'Brrrrraaaaaiiinz' and become zombies, and when two zombies meet they call 'huuuuunnnnngry', spreading until all are converted. Variation: use a vampire instead.

Object-work circle warm-up. One player silently molds an invisible ball of clay into a shape, optionally giving it a smell or emotion, then passes it left; the next acknowledges its weight, shape, and use, reforms it into a ball, makes a new object, and passes on, around the circle. Teaches that mime objects can carry narrative weight. Variations: Ball Pass (balls with different qualities), Object Circle (objects stay immutable).

Movement warm-up. One player leads and everyone falls in behind; the leader's repetitive movements cascade back through the line with delay and deterioration as each person copies the one directly ahead (not the leader). Embraces imperfection; useful in tight spaces. Variations: Aerobics (no layering), Flock Dance (pyramid), or the leader reversing so the last player becomes the new leader.

Synchronization circle warm-up. Players stand in a circle, eyes closed and heads down, and try to count from one to twenty as a group, each number said by a different player; if two speak at once they restart at one. Variations: 'Alphabet Circle' (letters) and 'Word at a Time' (a collaborative story that resets on overlap). Any group size.

Pass-and-copy circle warm-up. One player strikes an unconventional pose with a matching sound and passes both to their right-hand neighbor, who recreates them as accurately as possible before passing on; the gesture and sound travel fast around the circle, distorting as they go. Builds listening and acceptance of silliness.

Two-performer game (a variant of Helping Hands). One performer stands center with hands clasped behind their back while a second threads their arms through the first's armpits to supply mismatched arms; an interview by a host or another performer drives the scene as the body justifies the arms' actions. Variations: Legs Expert and Double Arms (two players each supply one arm).

Scene game. Performers play a normal open scene while a technician in the booth randomly inserts sound effects (door sounds, etc.) that the actors must justify into the story while still completing all the narrative beats. Variation: let an audience member operate the sound effects. 2+ performers.

Limitations scene game. The host assigns each performer a fixed number of words per sentence (standard numbers or playful values like zero, pi, or imaginary numbers) which they must obey all scene; counting on fingers is fine and helps the audience track it. Variation 'Rollercoaster': all share one word count that the host randomly changes mid-scene.

Performance game. The host assigns each performer a distinct emotion and conducts them like an orchestra by pointing; a pointed performer expresses their emotion, with the conductor's hand height setting intensity (low = mild, high = extreme), creating a rhythmic symphony of rising and fading emotions. Variations: Animal Symphony, Profession Symphony; gimmicks like pointing at several at once or rapidly changing one player's intensity.

Two-player scene game. Each performer is assigned a contrasting emotion (e.g. love vs anger) and they gradually exchange them over the scene, driven by elements of the narrative, so each ends on the other's starting emotion. Variation 'Status Transfer' applies the same gradual swap to character status instead of emotion.

Performance game. The stage is split into three sections, each assigned a genre by the host; as performers move across the boundaries they modify the story to the current zone's genre (sci-fi, soap opera, documentary, etc.), prioritizing narrative coherence over gags. Variations: emotional zones, animal zones, or genres assigned to characters rather than stage sections. Any number of performers.

Time-compression scene game (the Countdown family). Performers play a plain reference scene, then repeat the same content, arc, and dialogue in progressively shorter windows - 30 seconds, then 15, then 7. Variation 'Half Space' repeats the scene in a progressively smaller physical space instead of shorter time.

Performance game. The host recaps a historical event for the audience and performers enact it, with comedy coming from exploring and expanding the concepts behind the event rather than strict accuracy; players may add characters or reimagine elements while keeping the basic framework. Variations: skip the recap, modernize ancient events, or impose time limits.

Scene-switching game. Performers play an open scene that the host can interrupt at any time by calling 'Meanwhile!' plus a new setting; the players freeze and jump to the new location/scenario (first modeled by the host), then can return between scenes. Trains fast adaptation and seamless transitions. Related: What Happens Next? and And Now?

Performance game. Performers build a comedy scene with narrative and characters but play it deadpan; whenever a performer's actions make the audience laugh, the host removes them from the scene. The tone is subdued but the scene stays comedic; needs a host monitoring audience reactions.

Monologue game. Inspired by an audience-provided object, performers take turns delivering loosely connected individual character monologues, with new characters (not directly related to prior ones) replacing those on stage through standard transitions. Works as short-form or long-form, the longer version using subtler, deeper character development.

Audience-participation scene game. A host runs an open scene with arc and characters, periodically pausing to ask the audience for simple offers ('what does Leslie find in the fridge?') which the performers accept and weave in. Variations: Shopping List, Roller Coaster, Paper Chase (offers on scattered papers), and Hat/Bucket/Pocket (offers drawn from containers). Any number of performers.

An Options variant. Performers run an ongoing scene and occasionally bend to pick up slips of paper scattered on stage (audience-written before the show), read them aloud, and weave each offer into the existing narrative rather than tacking on tangents. Variations: draw offers from hats or buckets, or use images or physical actions as prompts.

Performance overlay on an open scene. The host cues individual players to take focus and deliver an overwrought, Academy-Award-acceptance-style soliloquy or monologue revealing character or story. Variations: technical awards (best lighting, best makeup) or absurd categories, or Shakespearean soliloquies instead of Oscar speeches. Any number of performers.

Scene played in full or near-darkness as a classic radio drama, where all action must be conveyed by word or sound effect since the audience can't see; challenging for physical performers. Variations: an online audio-cast/podcast version, or a longer-form version called 'Bat'. Any number of performers.

Audience-interruption game. During an open scene the audience can shout 'should have said' to force a performer to instantly replace their last line with something new, while the players keep the narrative coherent through the chaos. Variation 'Should Have Done' applies the same to actions and stage directions. Related to Ding/New Choice.

Overlay handle for open scenes. A performer suddenly breaks to monologue as if speaking to themselves while the others freeze and give focus; the soliloquy should deepen the narrative and reveal character rather than distract. Variation: 'Oscar Moment' plays the soliloquies campy and angst-filled.

Two-player game. Performers alternate between dialogue and stage directions: one says a line, the other states a stage direction that the first must execute, and so on, escalating from subtle to zany while keeping the scene coherent. Variations: elaborate descriptions, contradictory directions that oppose the dialogue, or emotionally revealing instructions.

Scene game. Performers periodically break dialogue to share their character's inner thoughts directly with the audience - which may contradict what they're saying aloud or add information - and the other players subtly incorporate that subconscious info. Variation: off-stage players voice the characters' subconscious (seeing or blind to the scene), possibly playing each other's inner monologues. Related to Asides.

Endowment performance game. Performers are called to eulogize a deceased superhero (introduced by the host); speakers - other heroes, villains, family, or sidekicks - deliver eulogies while receiving zany character endowments from the others, all building a story about the dead hero. Variations: endow speakers with physical constraints or mime-only speech; or an alternate version where heroes help a civilian.

Gibberish-translation game. A performer brings their new partner to meet their parents, who speak made-up gibberish; a translator conveys the parents' lines to the partner and audience while a typical family-meeting scene plays out. Stress full characters with movement and wants, not just the gimmick. Variations: translated opera, film versions, or a bad-translator scenario using real languages.

Gibberish musical game. On-stage performers sing an opera in a fabricated alien language, pausing after each gibberish line so off-stage translators interpret the 'sentence' for the audience; ideally the host assigns specific translators to specific singers. Variations: translators face away, use real languages with non-fluent speakers, or apply it to other scenarios like a medical encounter.

Line-up wit game. Players step forward in turn to deliver witty epitaphs or 'last words' for a host-given subject, riffing puns (e.g. a loaf of bread -> 'I am toast'). Can be competitive with the audience eliminating weak jokes. Variation 'Birth Notice' applies the same punning to humorous birth announcements.

Line-up wit game. The host names a mundane profession or noun and players step forward with pun one-liners in the form 'You know it's a [profession]'s offspring because...' (e.g. 'a plumber's offspring because she throws a wrench into everything'). Can be played with audience elimination; encourages clever wordplay over lazy stereotypes.

A-cappella musical game. Performers line up and sing a story one sentence at a time: the first sings solo then steps back to hum quiet backing as the next steps up with a new harmonizing line, layering into a multi-part unaccompanied arrangement; synchronizing the ending takes ensemble work. Variation 'Mangled Madrigal' uses set sentences the performers then riff off each other.

Scene-linking handle. A new scene's first spoken word must be the last word of the previous scene, though there's no obligation to keep the same characters or storyline; players can establish character and setting nonverbally before anyone speaks. Variations: use the last sentence or the last whole scene from the prior sketch. Any number of performers.

Replay handle. Performers play a neutral reference scene with simple dialogue, then replay it twice more, each time under a different overlay/endowment - traditionally film genres (sci-fi, etc.) but also emotions, occupations, or physical constraints; the host should consider the order of endowments. Variation 'Scene Many Ways' extends beyond three replays.

Ensemble exercise. About five linked players in a semicircle work to speak identical words simultaneously - starting from different phonemes, converging on a single sound, then on words sharing that sound ('slip', 'stop') - through listening, not following a leader. Variations: 'Date In One Voice' (two such groups converse) and 'Expert Scene' (a host interviews a unified expert).

Two-player limitations game. Each performer is secretly endowed with a different environment they must play their whole scene in (e.g. one checks a cake in a kitchen while the other mimes fixing a car in a garage), each believing the other shares their location; they must listen and accept to find overlapping mime objects that blend the worlds. Gimmick: three performers in three distinct environments.

Space-compression scene game. Players perform a scene using the full stage, then repeat the same content, actions, and narrative in progressively smaller spaces (halving the area each round) until they're literally on top of each other. Variation 'Half Life' applies the same halving to time instead of space.

Limitations handle. Performers run an open scene with a normal narrative arc and characters but speak exclusively in poetic verse with rhythm, syllables, and usually rhymes; advanced players co-write shared stanzas and couplets while beginners complete their own lines. 2+ players. Related to Verses and Rhymes.

Style overlay on an open scene parodying Shakespeare: players use his character archetypes (driven by guilt, jealousy, greed), Old English vocabulary ('alas', 'forsooth'), ideally iambic pentameter, and blend his tragedy and humor across the scene's arc, sound, setting, and dialogue.

Character-rotation game. When 'switch' is called, every performer takes over the character of the player to their right, and the rightmost player exits stage right; best with many players on stage for brisk comedic changes. Challenge: smooth, collision-free transitions while keeping the scene coherent. Variations: add a dead character for more movement, or switch sexes when rotating.

Nonverbal telephone endowment game for three. The three elements of a crime (place, person, item) are passed in order using only mime and gibberish, each performer guessing what the previous one communicated before passing it on; afterward the host quizzes them last-to-first. Variations: hints only, 30-second limits, or 'Chain Class Endowments' passing lecture notes before an exam.

Performance game. Two detectives examine a crime scene built from other performers and audience members frozen as human props, then build a narrative by trading offers to justify each position and explain how the crime happened, playing characters with a relationship and using small expansions. Variation: the audience guides the story with vocal reactions.

Time-pressure performance game. Performers act out a well-known movie plot in exactly 60 seconds; the host picks a famous, recognizable story and cuts lights at 60 seconds regardless of where they are, the comedy coming from the frantic pace. Variation 'Fairy Tale in a Minute' uses fairy tales instead.

Performance game (a Super Heroes relative). A civilian with a mundane problem calls in superheroes one at a time; each hero fails and another is summoned, until all the heroes decide to work together and solve it. 2+ performers. Variation 'Superhero Eulogy' uses the same format at a hero's funeral.

An Options variant. Performers run a scene and periodically turn to the audience, saying 'um err' with a questioning look, prompting the audience to shout suggestions that must be smoothly woven into the ongoing narrative. Variations: 'What Happens Next?' uses that phrase instead, and 'Google and Alexa' calls on imaginary AI assistants for suggestions.

A-cappella musical game. Performers line up and tell a story one sentence at a time: the first sings their line in the undulating, haunting tone of a plain chant then steps back while everyone repeats it together; each next performer sings the next logical sentence solo, echoed by the group, until the story ends and the ensemble trails into silence. Polyphonic variation: Madrigal (singing simultaneously).

Style handle. Performers retell a well-known fairy tale in a modern style set by an audience suggestion - a genre (sci-fi, horror, western), time period, political angle, or aesthetic - improvising the familiar story within the new frame. Works best when the cast knows the source tale, though unfamiliarity can add comedic chaos.

Limitations handle (a four-position Sitting Standing Lying). Performers run a scene where no two may occupy the same position at once; the audience buzzes whenever positions clash, forcing someone to change, and it works best with one fewer pose than performers for continuous repositioning. Gimmicks: unusual poses or performers getting trapped in a position.

Limitations game for 3+. Each performer gets a secret word from the host; when that word is spoken they must enter (if offstage) or exit (if onstage), but can't trigger their own word, and all movement must be justified in the story. Works best with a variety of word types (nouns, verbs, adjectives). Related to Walkout.

Conducted-story game for 4-5 in a line. A conductor points to indicate who narrates, and players must continue the story seamlessly mid-sentence or mid-word when switched to, sounding like one storyteller; the audience signals breaks with noise or a fail buzzer. Variations: Gibberish, Back Story (conductor taps from behind), and Word At A Time. A learnimprov framing of Story Story Die.

A Freeze Tag variant where, on 'freeze', any number of waiting performers can jump in at once, copying the frozen players' exact poses to start a new scene - 'chaos squared'. Any number of performers. Variations: Audience Freeze (spectators call the freeze) and Eyes Closed Freeze (replacements happen without seeing the pose).

Two groups of performers each form a single character that speaks one word at a time; the two clumps pass sentences back and forth, holding a conversation entirely word-at-a-time. Variation: fold in one or two audience members, supporting them so they look skilled.

Quick-wit warm-up. A center player points at someone and assigns a letter; that player must instantly make a sentence with a name, occupation, and location all starting with it ('Barney bakes bread in Baltimore'). The center rotates. Variations: non-geographical locations, or play in pairs exchanging alphabet letters. (Same family as Barney.)

Coordination circle warm-up. Players count '1-2-3-4' while progressively replacing each number with a gesture - touch head, shoulders, hips, knees - across five waves until the final wave is all movement and no speaking. Can be an elimination warm-up at speed. Variations: speed up, add harder gestures, or add more numbers and movements.

Concentration circle warm-up. Players stand with palms raised overhead; one gently pushes their right-hand neighbor's hand, sending a wave of pushes clockwise or counterclockwise around the group, and the leader can launch multiple waves until it's chaos. Builds listening and normalizes group failure. Variation 'Gate Controlled': wait for an incoming push to fully complete before pushing on.

Name-learning movement warm-up. Players take turns calling another player's name and crossing the circle to take their spot; the displaced player calls another name and moves, creating continuous motion. Builds movement, listening, and names. Variations: Cross Circle, Subtle Crossings (no pointing/names, eye contact only), Word at a Time (story words instead of names).

A category of calming, centering warm-ups before a show: Four Square Breathing (inhale/hold/exhale/hold for 4 counts each in cycles), Contract and Relax (tense and release muscle groups in turn, noting the sensation), and Thoughtful Meditation (guided visualization of a peaceful place using sensory detail). Any group size; especially useful before shows.
